questions.question_text: A liquid of density $600kg/m^{3}$ flowing steadily in a tube of varying cross-section. The cross-section at a point $A$ is $1.0cm^{2}$ and that at $B$ is $20mm^{2}$ . Both the points $A$ and $B$ are in same horizontal plane, the speed of the liquid at $A$ is $10cm/s$ . The difference in pressures at $A$ and $B$ points is $____$ Pa.
questions.question_html: A liquid of density $600kg/m^{3}$ flowing steadily in a tube of varying cross-section. The cross-section at a point $A$ is $1.0cm^{2}$ and that at $B$ is $20mm^{2}$ . Both the points $A$ and $B$ are in same horizontal plane, the speed of the liquid at $A$ is $10cm/s$ . The difference in pressures at $A$ and $B$ points is $____$ Pa.
questions.explanation_text: The density of liquid is $\rho=600kg/m^{3}$ . Area of cross-section at point A is $A_{A}=1.0cm^{2}=1.0 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$ . Area of cross-section at point $B$ is $A_{B}=20.0mm^{2}=20.0 \times 10^{-6}m^{2}=0.2 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$ . The velocity at A is $v_{A}=10cm/s=0.1m/s$ . For an incompressible liquid in steady flow, the mass flow rate must remain constant. Using equation of continuity, $A_{A}v_{A}=A_{B}v_{B}$ Substituting the values : $(1.0 \times 10^{-4}) \times (0.1)=(0.2 \times 10^{-4}) \times v_{B}$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_{B}=\frac{1.0 \times 0.1}{0.2}=\frac{0.1}{0.2}=0.5m/s$ According to Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal flow (where height $ℎ$ is constant), the sum of pressure and kinetic energy per unit volume is constant : $P_{A}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{A}^{2}=P_{B}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{B}^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $P_{A}-P_{B}=\Delta P_{AB}=\frac{1}{2}\rho(v_{B}^{2}-v_{A}^{2})$ Substituting the given values $\rho=600kg/m^{3},v_{B}=0.5m/s$ and $v_{A}=0.1m/s$ $P_{A}-P_{B}=\frac{1}{2} \times 600 \times (0.5^{2}-0.1^{2})$ $\Rightarrow$ $P_{A}-P_{B}=300 \times (0.25-0.01)$ $\Rightarrow$ $P_{A}-P_{B}=300 \times 0.24$ $\Rightarrow$ $P_{A}-P_{B}=72Pa$ Therefore, the difference in pressures at points A and B is 72 Pa . Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
The density of liquid is $\rho=600kg/m^{3}$ .

Area of cross-section at point A is $A_{A}=1.0cm^{2}=1.0 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$ .

Area of cross-section at point $B$ is $A_{B}=20.0mm^{2}=20.0 \times 10^{-6}m^{2}=0.2 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$ .

The velocity at A is $v_{A}=10cm/s=0.1m/s$ .

For an incompressible liquid in steady flow, the mass flow rate must remain constant.

Using equation of continuity,

$A_{A}v_{A}=A_{B}v_{B}$

Substituting the values :

$(1.0 \times 10^{-4}) \times (0.1)=(0.2 \times 10^{-4}) \times v_{B}$

$\Rightarrow$ $v_{B}=\frac{1.0 \times 0.1}{0.2}=\frac{0.1}{0.2}=0.5m/s$

According to Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal flow (where height $ℎ$ is constant), the sum of pressure and kinetic energy per unit volume is constant :

$P_{A}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{A}^{2}=P_{B}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{B}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $P_{A}-P_{B}=\Delta P_{AB}=\frac{1}{2}\rho(v_{B}^{2}-v_{A}^{2})$

Substituting the given values $\rho=600kg/m^{3},v_{B}=0.5m/s$ and $v_{A}=0.1m/s$

$P_{A}-P_{B}=\frac{1}{2} \times 600 \times (0.5^{2}-0.1^{2})$

$\Rightarrow$ $P_{A}-P_{B}=300 \times (0.25-0.01)$

$\Rightarrow$ $P_{A}-P_{B}=300 \times 0.24$

$\Rightarrow$ $P_{A}-P_{B}=72Pa$

Therefore, the difference in pressures at points A and B is 72 Pa .

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A lift of mass 1600 kg is supported by thick iron wire. If the maximum stress which the wire can withstand is $4 \times 10^{8}N/m^{2}$ and its radius is 4 mm , then maximum acceleration the lift can take is $____$ $m/s^{2}$ . (take $g=10m/s^{2}$ and $\pi=3.14$ )
questions.question_html:
A lift of mass 1600 kg is supported by thick iron wire. If the maximum stress which the wire can withstand is $4 \times 10^{8}N/m^{2}$ and its radius is 4 mm , then maximum acceleration the lift can take is $____$ $m/s^{2}$ .

(take $g=10m/s^{2}$ and $\pi=3.14$ )
questions.explanation_text: When a lift of mass M accelerates upward with acceleration a, the tension (T) in the supporting cable must overcome both gravity and provide the upward acceleration. Using Newton's Second Law ( $F_{\text{net}}=Ma$ ): $T-Mg=Ma \Rightarrow T=M(g+a)$ The stress $(\sigma)$ is defined as the restoring force (tension) per unit cross-sectional area (A): $\sigma=\frac{T}{A}=\frac{M(g+a)}{A}$ For a wire with a circular cross-section of radius r , the area of cross-section is $A=\pi r^{2}$ . $\sigma_{max}=\frac{M(g+a_{max})}{\pi r^{2}}$ The mass of lift is $M=1600kg$ The radius of cable is $r=4mm=4 \times 10^{-3}m$ So, the area is $A=\pi r^{2}=3.14 \times (4 \times 10^{-3})^{2}=3.14 \times 16 \times 10^{-6}m^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $A=50.24 \times 10^{-6}m^{2}$ So, the maximum stress is $\sigma_{max}=4 \times 10^{8}N/m^{2}$ From the maximum stress formula, $4 \times 10^{8}=\frac{1600(10+a_{max})}{50.24 \times 10^{-6}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $4 \times 10^{8} \times 50.24 \times 10^{-6}=1600(10+a_{max})$ $\Rightarrow$ $200.96 \times 10^{2}=1600(10+a_{max})$ $\Rightarrow$ $20096=1600(10+a_{max})$ $\Rightarrow$ $10+a_{max}=\frac{20096}{1600}=12.56$ $\Rightarrow$ $a_{max}=12.56-10=2.56m/s^{2}$ Therefore, the maximum acceleration of the lift is $2.56m/s^{2}$ . Thus, the correct option is (A).
questions.explanation_html:
When a lift of mass M accelerates upward with acceleration a, the tension (T) in the supporting cable must overcome both gravity and provide the upward acceleration.

Using Newton's Second Law ( $F_{\text{net}}=Ma$ ):

$T-Mg=Ma \Rightarrow T=M(g+a)$

The stress $(\sigma)$ is defined as the restoring force (tension) per unit cross-sectional area (A):

$\sigma=\frac{T}{A}=\frac{M(g+a)}{A}$

For a wire with a circular cross-section of radius r , the area of cross-section is $A=\pi r^{2}$ .

$\sigma_{max}=\frac{M(g+a_{max})}{\pi r^{2}}$

The mass of lift is $M=1600kg$

The radius of cable is $r=4mm=4 \times 10^{-3}m$

So, the area is

$A=\pi r^{2}=3.14 \times (4 \times 10^{-3})^{2}=3.14 \times 16 \times 10^{-6}m^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $A=50.24 \times 10^{-6}m^{2}$

So, the maximum stress is

$\sigma_{max}=4 \times 10^{8}N/m^{2}$

From the maximum stress formula,

$4 \times 10^{8}=\frac{1600(10+a_{max})}{50.24 \times 10^{-6}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $4 \times 10^{8} \times 50.24 \times 10^{-6}=1600(10+a_{max})$

$\Rightarrow$ $200.96 \times 10^{2}=1600(10+a_{max})$

$\Rightarrow$ $20096=1600(10+a_{max})$

$\Rightarrow$ $10+a_{max}=\frac{20096}{1600}=12.56$

$\Rightarrow$ $a_{max}=12.56-10=2.56m/s^{2}$

Therefore, the maximum acceleration of the lift is $2.56m/s^{2}$ .

Thus, the correct option is (A).

questions.question_text: Two wires as shown in the figure below, made of steel and have breaking stress of $12 \times 10^{8}N/m^{2}$ . Area of cross-section of upper wire is $0.008cm^{2}$ and of lower wire is $0.004cm^{2}$ . The maximum mass that can be added to pan without breaking any wire is $____$ kg.
questions.question_html: Two wires as shown in the figure below, made of steel and have breaking stress of $12 \times 10^{8}N/m^{2}$ . Area of cross-section of upper wire is $0.008cm^{2}$ and of lower wire is $0.004cm^{2}$ . The maximum mass that can be added to pan without breaking any wire is $____$ kg.
questions.explanation_text: Breaking tension ( $T_{max}$ ) is the maximum tension that can wire withstand without breaking. If the breaking stress of wire is $\sigma_{max}$ and area of cross-section is $A,\sigma_{max}=\frac{T_{max}}{A} \Rightarrow T_{max}=\sigma_{max} \times A$ For the lower wire the area of cross-section is $A_{L}=0.004cm^{2}=4 \times 10^{-7}m^{2}$ : $T_{L(max)}=(12 \times 10^{8}) \times (4 \times 10^{-7})=480N$ For the upper wire the area of cross-section is $A_{U}=0.008cm^{2}=8 \times 10^{-7}m^{2}$ : $T_{U(max)}=(12 \times 10^{8}) \times (8 \times 10^{-7})=960N$ Let M be the mass added to the pan. As lower wire supports the pan and the 10 kg mass. $T_{L}=(M+10)g=(M+10) \times 10$ For lower wire not to break: $10(M+10) \le 480 \Rightarrow M+10 \le 48 \Rightarrow M \le 38kg.....(ii)$ The upper wire supports the pan, 10 kg mass, and 30 kg mass. $T_{U}=(M+10+30)g=(M+40) \times 10$ For upper wire not to break: $10(M+40) \le 960 \Rightarrow M+40 \le 96 \Rightarrow M \le 56kg\dots(ii)$ To ensure neither wire breaks, we must choose the smaller of the two values. If we add 56 kg , the lower wire will break. If we add 38 kg , both wires remain intact. Therefore, the maximum load that can be placed in pan is 38 kg . Thus, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
Breaking tension ( $T_{max}$ ) is the maximum tension that can wire withstand without breaking.

If the breaking stress of wire is $\sigma_{max}$ and area of cross-section is $A,\sigma_{max}=\frac{T_{max}}{A} \Rightarrow T_{max}=\sigma_{max} \times A$

For the lower wire the area of cross-section is $A_{L}=0.004cm^{2}=4 \times 10^{-7}m^{2}$ :

$T_{L(max)}=(12 \times 10^{8}) \times (4 \times 10^{-7})=480N$

For the upper wire the area of cross-section is $A_{U}=0.008cm^{2}=8 \times 10^{-7}m^{2}$ :

$T_{U(max)}=(12 \times 10^{8}) \times (8 \times 10^{-7})=960N$

Let M be the mass added to the pan.

As lower wire supports the pan and the 10 kg mass.

$T_{L}=(M+10)g=(M+10) \times 10$

For lower wire not to break:

$10(M+10) \le 480 \Rightarrow M+10 \le 48 \Rightarrow M \le 38kg.....(ii)$

The upper wire supports the pan, 10 kg mass, and 30 kg mass.

$T_{U}=(M+10+30)g=(M+40) \times 10$

For upper wire not to break:

$10(M+40) \le 960 \Rightarrow M+40 \le 96 \Rightarrow M \le 56kg\dots(ii)$

To ensure neither wire breaks, we must choose the smaller of the two values. If we add 56 kg , the lower wire will break. If we add 38 kg , both wires remain intact. Therefore, the maximum load that can be placed in pan is 38 kg .

Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: A string $A$ of length 0.314 m and Young's modulus $2 \times 10^{10}N/m^{2}$ is connected to another string $B$ of length and Young's modulus both twice of those of $A$ . This series combination of strings is then suspended from a rigid support and its free end is fixed to a load of mass 0.8 kg . The net change in length of the combination is $____$ mm. (radius of both the strings is 0.2 mm and acceleration due to gravity $=10m/s^{2}$ ) (Mass of both strings is to be neglected as compared to the mass of load)
questions.question_html:
A string $A$ of length 0.314 m and Young's modulus $2 \times 10^{10}N/m^{2}$ is connected to another string $B$ of length and Young's modulus both twice of those of $A$ . This series combination of strings is then suspended from a rigid support and its free end is fixed to a load of mass 0.8 kg . The net change in length of the combination is $____$ mm.

(radius of both the strings is 0.2 mm and acceleration due to gravity $=10m/s^{2}$ ) (Mass of both strings is to be neglected as compared to the mass of load)
questions.explanation_text: Young's Modulus is defined as the ratio of longitudinal stress $(\sigma)$ to longitudinal strain $(\epsilon)$ : $Y=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}$ $\Delta L=\frac{FL}{AY}$ Where : F is the tension in the string ( $F=mg$ for a suspended load). L is the original length. A is the cross-sectional area ( $\pi r^{2}$ ). Y is the Young's Modulus. For String A The length of string is $L_{A}=0.314m \approx \frac{\pi}{10}m$ Young's modulus is $Y_{A}=2 \times 10^{10}N/m^{2}$ The radius of wire is $r=0.2mm=2 \times 10^{-4}m$ So, the area of string A is $A=\pi(2 \times 10^{-4})^{2}=4\pi \times 10^{-8}m^{2}$ The tensile force is $F=mg=0.8 \times 10=8N$ So, the elongation in string A is, $\Delta L_{A}=\frac{8 \times 0.314}{(4\pi \times 10^{-8}) \times (2 \times 10^{10})}$ Using $0.314 \approx \frac{\pi}{10}$ : $\Delta L_{A}=\frac{8 \times (\frac{\pi}{10})}{8\pi \times 10^{2}}=\frac{\pi}{10 \times \pi \times 10^{2}}=10^{-3}m=1mm$ For string B It is given that $L_{B}=2L_{A}$ and $Y_{B}=2Y_{A}$ , while $F$ and $A$ remain the same: $\Delta L_{B}=\frac{F(2L_{A})}{A(2Y_{A})}=\frac{FL_{A}}{AY_{A}}=\Delta L_{A}$ So, $\Delta L_{B}=1mm$ . Hence, the total elongation of the combination is, $\Delta L_{\text{total}}=\Delta L_{A}+\Delta L_{B}=1mm+1mm=2mm$ Therefore, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
Young's Modulus is defined as the ratio of longitudinal stress $(\sigma)$ to longitudinal strain $(\epsilon)$ :

$Y=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}$

$\Delta L=\frac{FL}{AY}$

Where :

  • F is the tension in the string ( $F=mg$ for a suspended load).

  • L is the original length.

  • A is the cross-sectional area ( $\pi r^{2}$ ).

  • Y is the Young's Modulus.

For String A

The length of string is $L_{A}=0.314m \approx \frac{\pi}{10}m$

Young's modulus is $Y_{A}=2 \times 10^{10}N/m^{2}$

The radius of wire is $r=0.2mm=2 \times 10^{-4}m$

So, the area of string A is $A=\pi(2 \times 10^{-4})^{2}=4\pi \times 10^{-8}m^{2}$

The tensile force is $F=mg=0.8 \times 10=8N$

So, the elongation in string A is,

$\Delta L_{A}=\frac{8 \times 0.314}{(4\pi \times 10^{-8}) \times (2 \times 10^{10})}$

Using $0.314 \approx \frac{\pi}{10}$ :

$\Delta L_{A}=\frac{8 \times (\frac{\pi}{10})}{8\pi \times 10^{2}}=\frac{\pi}{10 \times \pi \times 10^{2}}=10^{-3}m=1mm$

For string B

It is given that $L_{B}=2L_{A}$ and $Y_{B}=2Y_{A}$ , while $F$ and $A$ remain the same:

$\Delta L_{B}=\frac{F(2L_{A})}{A(2Y_{A})}=\frac{FL_{A}}{AY_{A}}=\Delta L_{A}$

So, $\Delta L_{B}=1mm$ .

Hence, the total elongation of the combination is,

$\Delta L_{\text{total}}=\Delta L_{A}+\Delta L_{B}=1mm+1mm=2mm$

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: Two wires $A$ and $B$ made of different materials of lengths 6.0 cm and 5.4 cm , respectively and area of cross sections $3.0 \times 10^{-5}m^{2}$ and $4.5 \times 10^{-5}m^{2}$ , respectively are stretched by the same magnitude under a given load. The ratio of the Young's modulus of $A$ to that of $B$ is $x:3$ . The value of $x$ is $____$
questions.question_html: Two wires $A$ and $B$ made of different materials of lengths 6.0 cm and 5.4 cm , respectively and area of cross sections $3.0 \times 10^{-5}m^{2}$ and $4.5 \times 10^{-5}m^{2}$ , respectively are stretched by the same magnitude under a given load. The ratio of the Young's modulus of $A$ to that of $B$ is $x:3$ . The value of $x$ is $____$
questions.explanation_text: Young's Modulus is given by : $Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}=\frac{FL}{A\Delta L}$ Where: F is the applied force (load) L is the original length. A is the area of cross-section $\Delta L$ is the change in length (stretching) According to question, both wires are stretched by the same magnitude ( $\Delta L_{A}=\Delta L_{B}$ ) under the same given load $(F_{A}=F_{B})$ . Therefore, for both wires: $Y∝\frac{L}{A}$ Let $Y_{A}$ and $Y_{B}$ be the Young's moduli for wires $A$ and $B$ : $\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{(\frac{L_{A}}{A_{A}})}{(\frac{L_{B}}{A_{B}})}=\frac{L_{A}}{L_{B}} \times \frac{A_{B}}{A_{A}}$ The given values : $L_{A}=6.0cm,L_{B}=5.4cm$ $A_{A}=3.0 \times 10^{-5}m^{2},A_{B}=4.5 \times 10^{-5}m^{2}$ $\begin{aligned} \frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{6.0}{5.4} \times \frac{4.5 \times 10^{-5}}{3.0 \times 10^{-5}} \\ \frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{5}{3}=\frac{x}{3} \Rightarrow x=5 \end{aligned}$ So, the value of x is 5 . Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
Young's Modulus is given by :

$Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}=\frac{FL}{A\Delta L}$

Where:

  • F is the applied force (load)

  • L is the original length.

  • A is the area of cross-section

  • $\Delta L$ is the change in length (stretching)

According to question, both wires are stretched by the same magnitude ( $\Delta L_{A}=\Delta L_{B}$ ) under the same given load $(F_{A}=F_{B})$ .

Therefore, for both wires:

$Y∝\frac{L}{A}$

Let $Y_{A}$ and $Y_{B}$ be the Young's moduli for wires $A$ and $B$ :

$\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{(\frac{L_{A}}{A_{A}})}{(\frac{L_{B}}{A_{B}})}=\frac{L_{A}}{L_{B}} \times \frac{A_{B}}{A_{A}}$

The given values :

  • $L_{A}=6.0cm,L_{B}=5.4cm$

  • $A_{A}=3.0 \times 10^{-5}m^{2},A_{B}=4.5 \times 10^{-5}m^{2}$

$\begin{aligned} \frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{6.0}{5.4} \times \frac{4.5 \times 10^{-5}}{3.0 \times 10^{-5}} \\ \frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{5}{3}=\frac{x}{3} \Rightarrow x=5 \end{aligned}$

So, the value of x is 5 . Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: The strain-stress plot for materials $A,B,C$ and $D$ is shown in the figure. Which material has the largest Young's modulus ?
questions.question_html: The strain-stress plot for materials $A,B,C$ and $D$ is shown in the figure. Which material has the largest Young's modulus ?
questions.explanation_text: Young's Modulus (Y) is defined as the ratio of Stress $(\sigma)$ to Strain $(\epsilon)$ within the elastic limit : $Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}$ For the given graph, 1. Y -axis: $Strain(\epsilon)$ 2. X -axis: Stress $(\sigma)$ Since Strain is on the Y -axis and Stress is on the X -axis, the slope of the line is given by : $\text{Slope}=\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}=\frac{\text{Strain}}{\text{Stress}}$ $\text{Slope}=\frac{1}{Y}$ It shows that the slope is inversely proportional to Young's Modulus, i.e., higher slope corresponds to smaller Young's Modulus (material is more elastic) whereas lower slope shows larger Young's Modulus (material is less elastic). So, the material with the largest Young's modulus will be the line with the smallest slope. 1. Material A has the highest slope → smallest Y. 2. Material C has the lowest slope → largest Y. Therefore, material C has the largest Young's modulus. Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
Young's Modulus (Y) is defined as the ratio of Stress $(\sigma)$ to Strain $(\epsilon)$ within the elastic limit :

$Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}$

For the given graph,

  • 1. Y -axis: $Strain(\epsilon)$

  • 2. X -axis: Stress $(\sigma)$

Since Strain is on the Y -axis and Stress is on the X -axis, the slope of the line is given by :

$\text{Slope}=\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}=\frac{\text{Strain}}{\text{Stress}}$

$\text{Slope}=\frac{1}{Y}$

It shows that the slope is inversely proportional to Young's Modulus, i.e., higher slope corresponds to smaller Young's Modulus (material is more elastic) whereas lower slope shows larger Young's Modulus (material is less elastic).

So, the material with the largest Young's modulus will be the line with the smallest slope.

  • 1. Material A has the highest slope → smallest Y.

  • 2. Material C has the lowest slope → largest Y.

Therefore, material C has the largest Young's modulus. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: An aluminium and steel rods having same lengths and cross-sections are joined to make total length of 120 cm at $30^{\circ}C$ . The coefficient of linear expansion of aluminium and steel are $24 \times 10^{-6}/^{\circ}C$ and $1.2 \times 10^{-5}/^{\circ}C$ , respectively. The length of this composite rod when its temperature is raised to $100^{\circ}C$ , is $____$ cm.
questions.question_html: An aluminium and steel rods having same lengths and cross-sections are joined to make total length of 120 cm at $30^{\circ}C$ . The coefficient of linear expansion of aluminium and steel are $24 \times 10^{-6}/^{\circ}C$ and $1.2 \times 10^{-5}/^{\circ}C$ , respectively. The length of this composite rod when its temperature is raised to $100^{\circ}C$ , is $____$ cm.
questions.explanation_text: To find the final length of the composite rod, we need to calculate the expansion of both the aluminium and steel sections individually and then add them to the original length. Total Initial Length $(L_{1})$ is 120 cm at $30^{\circ}C$ . Since both rods have the same length, the initial length of each rod is, $L_{Al}=\frac{120}{2}=60cm$ and $L_{St}=\frac{120}{2}=$ 60 cm . The change in temperature is, $\Delta T=T_{\text{final}}-T_{\text{initial}}=100^{\circ}C-30^{\circ}C=70^{\circ}C$ Coefficients of linear expansion ( $\alpha$ ) for aluminium is $\alpha_{Al}=24 \times 10^{-6}/^{\circ}C$ and that for steel is $\alpha_{St}=1.2 \times 10^{-5}/^{\circ}C=12 \times 10^{-6}/^{\circ}C$ . The linear expansion is $\Delta L=L_{\text{initial}} \cdot \alpha \cdot \Delta T$ For Aluminium : $\Delta L_{Al}=60 \times (24 \times 10^{-6}) \times 70$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta L_{Al}=60 \times 70 \times 24 \times 10^{-6}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta L_{Al}=4200 \times 24 \times 10^{-6}=100800 \times 10^{-6}=0.1008cm$ For Steel : $\Delta L_{St}=60 \times (12 \times 10^{-6}) \times 70$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta L_{St}=4200 \times 12 \times 10^{-6}=50400 \times 10^{-6}=0.0504cm$ The total change in length ( $\Delta L_{\text{total}}$ ) is : $\Delta L_{\text{total}}=\Delta L_{Al}+\Delta L_{St}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta L_{\text{total}}=0.1008+0.0504=0.1512cm$ So, the final length of the rod is : $L_{final}=120+0.1512=120.1512cm$ $\Rightarrow$ $L_{final} \approx 120.15cm$ Therefore, the final length of the combination is 120.15 cm . Hence, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
To find the final length of the composite rod, we need to calculate the expansion of both the aluminium and steel sections individually and then add them to the original length.

Total Initial Length $(L_{1})$ is 120 cm at $30^{\circ}C$ .

Since both rods have the same length, the initial length of each rod is, $L_{Al}=\frac{120}{2}=60cm$ and $L_{St}=\frac{120}{2}=$ 60 cm .

The change in temperature is,

$\Delta T=T_{\text{final}}-T_{\text{initial}}=100^{\circ}C-30^{\circ}C=70^{\circ}C$

Coefficients of linear expansion ( $\alpha$ ) for aluminium is $\alpha_{Al}=24 \times 10^{-6}/^{\circ}C$ and that for steel is $\alpha_{St}=1.2 \times 10^{-5}/^{\circ}C=12 \times 10^{-6}/^{\circ}C$ .

The linear expansion is $\Delta L=L_{\text{initial}} \cdot \alpha \cdot \Delta T$

For Aluminium :

$\Delta L_{Al}=60 \times (24 \times 10^{-6}) \times 70$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta L_{Al}=60 \times 70 \times 24 \times 10^{-6}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta L_{Al}=4200 \times 24 \times 10^{-6}=100800 \times 10^{-6}=0.1008cm$

For Steel :

$\Delta L_{St}=60 \times (12 \times 10^{-6}) \times 70$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta L_{St}=4200 \times 12 \times 10^{-6}=50400 \times 10^{-6}=0.0504cm$

The total change in length ( $\Delta L_{\text{total}}$ ) is :

$\Delta L_{\text{total}}=\Delta L_{Al}+\Delta L_{St}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta L_{\text{total}}=0.1008+0.0504=0.1512cm$

So, the final length of the rod is :

$L_{final}=120+0.1512=120.1512cm$

$\Rightarrow$ $L_{final} \approx 120.15cm$

Therefore, the final length of the combination is 120.15 cm .

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.question_text: The surface tension of a soap solution is $3.5 \times 10^{-2}N/m$ . The work required to increase the radius of a soap bubble from 1 cm to 2 cm is $\alpha \times 10^{-6}J$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ . $(\pi=22/7)$
questions.question_html:
The surface tension of a soap solution is $3.5 \times 10^{-2}N/m$ . The work required to increase the radius of a soap bubble from 1 cm to 2 cm is $\alpha \times 10^{-6}J$ . The value of $\alpha$ is $____$ .

$(\pi=22/7)$
questions.explanation_text: A soap bubble has two free surfaces (an inner surface and an outer surface). questions.question_text: Sixty four rain drops of radius 1 mm each falling down with a terminal velocity of $10cm/s$ coalesce to form a bigger drop. The terminal velocity of bigger drop is $____$ $cm/s$ .
questions.question_html:
Sixty four rain drops of radius 1 mm each falling down with a terminal velocity of $10cm/s$ coalesce to form a bigger drop. The terminal velocity of bigger drop is

$____$ $cm/s$ .
questions.explanation_text: When a spherical drop falls through a viscous medium (like air), it reaches a constant speed called terminal velocity $(v_{t})$ when the net force on it is zero. The forces involved are : Weight ( W ) is acting downwards, $W=mg=$ Volume $\times \rho \times g$ . Buoyant force ( $F_{b}$ ) is acting upwards. Viscous drag force ( $F_{v}$ ) is acting upwards According to Stokes' Law $F_{v}=6\pi\eta r$ v. At equilibrium, the net force must be zero. $W-F_{b}=F_{v}$ This leads to the standard formula for terminal velocity : $v_{t}=\frac{2r^{2}g(\rho-\sigma)}{9\eta}$ Where : $r=$ Radius of the drop $\rho=$ Density of the drop (water) $\sigma=$ Density of the medium (air) $\eta=$ Coefficient of viscosity $g=$ Acceleration due to gravity Since $g,\rho,\sigma$ , and $\eta$ are constants for both the small and big drops, the terminal velocity is directly proportional to the square of the radius. $v_{t}∝r^{2}$ When 64 small drops combine to form one big drop, the total volume remains conserved. Let r be the radius of a small drop. Let R be the radius of the big drop. Let $n=64$ be the number of drops. Volume of Big Drop $=n \times$ (Volume of Small Drop) $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}=n \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $R^{3}=n \cdot r^{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $R=n^{1/3} \cdot r$ Substituting $n=64$ : $R=64^{1/3} \cdot r$ $\Rightarrow$ $R=4r$ So, the ratio of the terminal velocities for big and small drop using the fact that terminal velocity is proportional to square of radius, $\frac{v_{\text{big}}}{v_{\text{small}}}=\frac{R^{2}}{r^{2}}=(\frac{R}{r})^{2}=(\frac{4r}{4})^{2}=16$ Given $v_{\text{small}}=10cm/s$ . $v_{\text{big}}=16 \times v_{\text{small}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_{big}=16 \times 10cm/s$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_{big}=160cm/s$
questions.explanation_html:
When a spherical drop falls through a viscous medium (like air), it reaches a constant speed called terminal velocity $(v_{t})$ when the net force on it is zero.

The forces involved are :

Weight ( W ) is acting downwards, $W=mg=$ Volume $\times \rho \times g$ .

Buoyant force ( $F_{b}$ ) is acting upwards.

Viscous drag force ( $F_{v}$ ) is acting upwards

According to Stokes' Law $F_{v}=6\pi\eta r$ v.

At equilibrium, the net force must be zero.

$W-F_{b}=F_{v}$

This leads to the standard formula for terminal velocity :

$v_{t}=\frac{2r^{2}g(\rho-\sigma)}{9\eta}$

Where :

  • $r=$ Radius of the drop

  • $\rho=$ Density of the drop (water)

  • $\sigma=$ Density of the medium (air)

  • $\eta=$ Coefficient of viscosity

  • $g=$ Acceleration due to gravity

Since $g,\rho,\sigma$ , and $\eta$ are constants for both the small and big drops, the terminal velocity is directly proportional to the square of the radius.

$v_{t}∝r^{2}$

When 64 small drops combine to form one big drop, the total volume remains conserved.

  • Let r be the radius of a small drop.

  • Let R be the radius of the big drop.

  • Let $n=64$ be the number of drops.

Volume of Big Drop $=n \times$ (Volume of Small Drop)

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}=n \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $R^{3}=n \cdot r^{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $R=n^{1/3} \cdot r$

Substituting $n=64$ :

$R=64^{1/3} \cdot r$

$\Rightarrow$ $R=4r$

So, the ratio of the terminal velocities for big and small drop using the fact that terminal velocity is proportional to square of radius,

$\frac{v_{\text{big}}}{v_{\text{small}}}=\frac{R^{2}}{r^{2}}=(\frac{R}{r})^{2}=(\frac{4r}{4})^{2}=16$

Given $v_{\text{small}}=10cm/s$ .

$v_{\text{big}}=16 \times v_{\text{small}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $v_{big}=16 \times 10cm/s$

$\Rightarrow$ $v_{big}=160cm/s$

questions.question_text: A spherical liquid drop of radius $R$ acquires the terminal velocity $v_{1}$ when falls through a gas of viscosity $\eta$ . Now the drop is broken into 64 identical droplets and each droplet acquires terminal velocity $v_{2}$ falling through the same gas. The ratio of terminal velocities $v_{1}/v_{2}$ is $____$ .
questions.question_html: A spherical liquid drop of radius $R$ acquires the terminal velocity $v_{1}$ when falls through a gas of viscosity $\eta$ . Now the drop is broken into 64 identical droplets and each droplet acquires terminal velocity $v_{2}$ falling through the same gas. The ratio of terminal velocities $v_{1}/v_{2}$ is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: When a spherical object falls through a viscous fluid, it eventually reaches a constant speed called terminal velocity $(v_{t})$ . This occurs when the downward force of gravity is balanced by the upward buoyant force and the viscous drag force. The force of gravity acting on the sphere is $F_{g}=mg=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\rho g$ , where $\rho$ is the density of the liquid. Using Archimedean's principle of buoyant force $F_{b}=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\sigma g$ , where $\sigma$ is the density of the gas. Using Stokes' Law the viscous drag is $F_{v}=6\pi\eta rv_{t}$ At terminal velocity, $F_{v}=F_{g}-F_{b}$ $\Rightarrow$ $6\pi\eta rv_{t}=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}(\rho-\sigma)g$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_{t}=\frac{2r^{2}(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta}$ For the same liquid and gas, terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius : $v∝r^{2}$ The large drop of radius $R$ is broken into 64 identical droplets of radius $r$ . Since the total volume remains constant : $V_{R}=64 \times V_{r}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}=64 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $R^{3}=64r^{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $R=4r \Rightarrow r=\frac{R}{4}$ Let $v_{1}$ be the terminal velocity of the large drop and $v_{2}$ be the terminal velocity of a small droplet. Using the relationship $v∝r^{2}$ : $\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=\frac{R^{2}}{r^{2}}$ Substituting $r=\frac{R}{4}$ : $\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=\frac{R^{2}}{(\frac{R}{4})^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=\frac{R^{2}}{R^{2}/16}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=16$ Therefore, the ratio of terminal velocities $\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}$ is 16 . Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
When a spherical object falls through a viscous fluid, it eventually reaches a constant speed called terminal velocity $(v_{t})$ . This occurs when the downward force of gravity is balanced by the upward buoyant force and the viscous drag force.

The force of gravity acting on the sphere is $F_{g}=mg=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\rho g$ , where $\rho$ is the density of the liquid.

Using Archimedean's principle of buoyant force $F_{b}=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\sigma g$ , where $\sigma$ is the density of the gas.

Using Stokes' Law the viscous drag is $F_{v}=6\pi\eta rv_{t}$

At terminal velocity,

$F_{v}=F_{g}-F_{b}$

$\Rightarrow$ $6\pi\eta rv_{t}=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}(\rho-\sigma)g$

$\Rightarrow$ $v_{t}=\frac{2r^{2}(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta}$

For the same liquid and gas, terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius :

$v∝r^{2}$

The large drop of radius $R$ is broken into 64 identical droplets of radius $r$ . Since the total volume remains constant :

$V_{R}=64 \times V_{r}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}=64 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $R^{3}=64r^{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $R=4r \Rightarrow r=\frac{R}{4}$

Let $v_{1}$ be the terminal velocity of the large drop and $v_{2}$ be the terminal velocity of a small droplet. Using the relationship $v∝r^{2}$ :

$\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=\frac{R^{2}}{r^{2}}$

Substituting $r=\frac{R}{4}$ :

$\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=\frac{R^{2}}{(\frac{R}{4})^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=\frac{R^{2}}{R^{2}/16}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=16$

Therefore, the ratio of terminal velocities $\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}$ is 16 .

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: The two wires $A$ and $B$ of equal cross-section but of different materials are joined together. The ratio of Young's modulus of wire $A$ and wire $B$ is 20/11. When the joined wire is kept under certain tension the elongations in the wires $A$ and $B$ are equal. If the length of wire $A$ is 2.2 m , then the length of wire $B$ is $____$ m.
questions.question_html:
The two wires $A$ and $B$ of equal cross-section but of different materials are joined together. The ratio of Young's modulus of wire $A$ and wire $B$ is 20/11. When the joined wire is kept under certain tension the elongations in the wires $A$ and $B$ are equal. If the length of wire $A$ is 2.2 m , then the length of wire $B$ is

$____$ m.
questions.explanation_text: Young's Modulus is defined as the ratio of Stress $(\sigma)$ to Strain $(\epsilon)$ . $Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}$ Stress is force per unit area, $\sigma=\frac{\text{Force (F)}}{\text{Area (A)}}$ Strain is change in length per unit original length, $\epsilon=\frac{\text{Change in length}(\Delta L)}{\text{Original length}(L)}$ So, $Y=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}$ $\Rightarrow \Delta L=\frac{FL}{AY}$ Since the wires are joined in series and kept under tension, the Force (F) acting on both wires is the same. The area (A) is the same for both. It is given that the elongation in both the wires is equal, $\Delta L_{A}=\Delta L_{B}$ . Since $\Delta L_{A}=\Delta L_{B}:$ $\frac{FL_{A}}{AY_{A}}=\frac{FL_{B}}{AY_{B}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{L_{A}}{Y_{A}}=\frac{L_{B}}{Y_{B}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{L_{A}}{L_{B}}=\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}$ The ratio of Young's modulus is $\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{20}{11}$ and the length of wire $A$ is $L_{A}=2.2m$ $\frac{2.2}{L_{B}}=\frac{20}{11}$ $\Rightarrow$ $L_{B}=2.2 \times \frac{11}{20}$ $\Rightarrow$ $L_{B}=\frac{24.2}{20}$ $\Rightarrow$ $L_{B}=1.21m$ Therefore, the length of wire B is 1.21 m . Hence, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
Young's Modulus is defined as the ratio of Stress $(\sigma)$ to Strain $(\epsilon)$ .

$Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}$

Stress is force per unit area, $\sigma=\frac{\text{Force (F)}}{\text{Area (A)}}$

Strain is change in length per unit original length,

$\epsilon=\frac{\text{Change in length}(\Delta L)}{\text{Original length}(L)}$

So, $Y=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}$

$\Rightarrow \Delta L=\frac{FL}{AY}$

Since the wires are joined in series and kept under tension, the Force (F) acting on both wires is the same.

The area (A) is the same for both.

It is given that the elongation in both the wires is equal, $\Delta L_{A}=\Delta L_{B}$ .

Since $\Delta L_{A}=\Delta L_{B}:$

$\frac{FL_{A}}{AY_{A}}=\frac{FL_{B}}{AY_{B}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{L_{A}}{Y_{A}}=\frac{L_{B}}{Y_{B}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{L_{A}}{L_{B}}=\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}$

The ratio of Young's modulus is $\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{20}{11}$ and the length of wire $A$ is $L_{A}=2.2m$

$\frac{2.2}{L_{B}}=\frac{20}{11}$

$\Rightarrow$ $L_{B}=2.2 \times \frac{11}{20}$

$\Rightarrow$ $L_{B}=\frac{24.2}{20}$

$\Rightarrow$ $L_{B}=1.21m$

Therefore, the length of wire B is 1.21 m . Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.question_text: A metal string $A$ is suspended from a rigid support and its free end is attached to a block of mass $M$ . Second block having mass 2 M is suspended at the bottom of the first block using a string $B$ . The area of cross sections of strings $A$ and $B$ are same. The ratio of lengths of strings of $A$ to B is 2 and the ratio of their Young's moduli $(Y_{A}/Y_{B})$ is 0.5 . The ratio of elongations in $A$ to $B$ is $____$ .
questions.question_html: A metal string $A$ is suspended from a rigid support and its free end is attached to a block of mass $M$ . Second block having mass 2 M is suspended at the bottom of the first block using a string $B$ . The area of cross sections of strings $A$ and $B$ are same. The ratio of lengths of strings of $A$ to B is 2 and the ratio of their Young's moduli $(Y_{A}/Y_{B})$ is 0.5 . The ratio of elongations in $A$ to $B$ is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: Young's Modulus (Y) is defined as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain : $Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta L=\frac{FL}{AY}\dots(ii)$ Where, F is the tension in the string, L is the original length, A is the area of cross-section. Y is the Young's Modulus. For string B This string supports only the bottom block of mass 2 M . $F_{B}=2Mg$ For string A This string supports both mass M and the mass 2 M hanging below it. $F_{A}=Mg+2Mg=3Mg$ The ratio of lengths is $\frac{L_{A}}{L_{B}}=2$ The ratio of Young's moduli is $\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=0.5$ . The areas are same, $A_{A}=A_{B}=A$ . Using the formula of extension in string (i), $\frac{\Delta L_{A}}{\Delta L_{B}}=\frac{F_{A}L_{A}/A_{A}Y_{A}}{F_{B}L_{B}/A_{B}Y_{B}}=(\frac{F_{A}}{F_{B}}) \times (\frac{L_{A}}{L_{B}})(\frac{Y_{B}}{Y_{A}})$ Substituting the values : $\frac{\Delta L_{A}}{\Delta L_{B}}=(\frac{3Mg}{2Mg}) \times (2) \times (\frac{1}{0.5})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\Delta L_{A}}{\Delta L_{B}}=(\frac{3}{2}) \times 2 \times 2$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\Delta L_{A}}{\Delta L_{B}}=3 \times 2=6$ Therefore, the ratio of elongations in A to B is 6. Thus, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
Young's Modulus (Y) is defined as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain :

$Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta L=\frac{FL}{AY}\dots(ii)$

Where, F is the tension in the string, L is the original length, A is the area of cross-section. Y is the Young's Modulus.

For string B

This string supports only the bottom block of mass 2 M .

$F_{B}=2Mg$

For string A

This string supports both mass M and the mass 2 M hanging below it.

$F_{A}=Mg+2Mg=3Mg$

The ratio of lengths is $\frac{L_{A}}{L_{B}}=2$

The ratio of Young's moduli is $\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=0.5$ .

The areas are same, $A_{A}=A_{B}=A$ .

Using the formula of extension in string (i),

$\frac{\Delta L_{A}}{\Delta L_{B}}=\frac{F_{A}L_{A}/A_{A}Y_{A}}{F_{B}L_{B}/A_{B}Y_{B}}=(\frac{F_{A}}{F_{B}}) \times (\frac{L_{A}}{L_{B}})(\frac{Y_{B}}{Y_{A}})$

Substituting the values :

$\frac{\Delta L_{A}}{\Delta L_{B}}=(\frac{3Mg}{2Mg}) \times (2) \times (\frac{1}{0.5})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\Delta L_{A}}{\Delta L_{B}}=(\frac{3}{2}) \times 2 \times 2$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\Delta L_{A}}{\Delta L_{B}}=3 \times 2=6$

Therefore, the ratio of elongations in A to B is 6.

Thus, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: The surface tension of a soap bubble is 0.03 N/m. The work done in increasing the diameter of bubble from 2 cm to 6 cm is $\alpha\pi \times 10^{-4}$ J. The value of $\alpha$ is _________. (Take $\pi=3.14$ )
questions.question_html: The surface tension of a soap bubble is 0.03 N/m. The work done in increasing the diameter of bubble from 2 cm to 6 cm is $\alpha\pi \times 10^{-4}$ J. The value of $\alpha$ is _________. (Take $\pi=3.14$ )
questions.explanation_text: Work done in increasing the size of a soap bubble is stored as surface energy. A soap bubble has two free surfaces (the inner and the outer air-liquid interfaces). The work done W is given by : $W=T \times (2 \times \Delta A)$ Where T is surface tension and $\Delta A$ is the change in area of one surface $\Delta A=(4\pi R_{2}^{2}-4\pi R_{1}^{2})$ Putting the expression in work done, $W=2T \times 4\pi(R_{2}^{2}-R_{1}^{2})=8\pi T(R_{2}^{2}-R_{1}^{2})$ The surface tension of soap bubble is $T=0.03N/m$ The initial diameter is $D_{1}=2cm \Rightarrow R_{1}=1cm=1 \times 10^{-2}m$ The final diameter is $D_{2}=6cm \Rightarrow R_{2}=3cm=3 \times 10^{-2}m$ Substitute the values into the expression for work done : $W=8\pi(0.03)[(3 \times 10^{-2})^{2}-(1 \times 10^{-2})^{2}]$ $\Rightarrow$ $W=0.24\pi[9 \times 10^{-4}-1 \times 10^{-4}]$ $\Rightarrow$ $W=0.24\pi[8 \times 10^{-4}]$ $\Rightarrow$ $W=1.92\pi \times 10^{-4}J=\alpha\pi \times 10^{-4}J$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=1.92$ Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is 1.92 . Hence, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
Work done in increasing the size of a soap bubble is stored as surface energy.

A soap bubble has two free surfaces (the inner and the outer air-liquid interfaces). The work done W is given by :

$W=T \times (2 \times \Delta A)$

Where T is surface tension and $\Delta A$ is the change in area of one surface

$\Delta A=(4\pi R_{2}^{2}-4\pi R_{1}^{2})$

Putting the expression in work done,

$W=2T \times 4\pi(R_{2}^{2}-R_{1}^{2})=8\pi T(R_{2}^{2}-R_{1}^{2})$

The surface tension of soap bubble is $T=0.03N/m$

The initial diameter is $D_{1}=2cm \Rightarrow R_{1}=1cm=1 \times 10^{-2}m$

The final diameter is $D_{2}=6cm \Rightarrow R_{2}=3cm=3 \times 10^{-2}m$

Substitute the values into the expression for work done :

$W=8\pi(0.03)[(3 \times 10^{-2})^{2}-(1 \times 10^{-2})^{2}]$

$\Rightarrow$ $W=0.24\pi[9 \times 10^{-4}-1 \times 10^{-4}]$

$\Rightarrow$ $W=0.24\pi[8 \times 10^{-4}]$

$\Rightarrow$ $W=1.92\pi \times 10^{-4}J=\alpha\pi \times 10^{-4}J$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=1.92$

Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is 1.92 .

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.question_text: A cubical block of density $\rho_{b}=600kg/m^{3}$ floats in a liquid of density $\rho_{e}=900kg/m^{3}$ . If the height of block is $H=8.0cm$ then height of the submerged part is $____$ cm .
questions.question_html:
A cubical block of density $\rho_{b}=600kg/m^{3}$ floats in a liquid of density $\rho_{e}=900kg/m^{3}$ . If the height of block is $H=8.0cm$ then height of the submerged part is

$____$ cm .
questions.explanation_text: When an object floats in a liquid, the weight of the object is exactly balanced by the buoyant force (up thrust) exerted by the liquid. Weight of block is $=W=m \cdot g=(\rho_{b} \times V_{\text{total}}) \times g$ Buoyant force ( $F_{B}$ ) acting on a submerged body is equal to the weight of displaced liquid, $F_{B}=(\rho_{1}V_{\text{submerged}}) \times g$ For flotation : $W=F_{B}$ $\rho_{b}V_{\text{total}}g=\rho_{l}V_{\text{submerged}}g$ For a cubical block with a uniform cross-sectional area (A): Total Volume $=V_{\text{total}}=AH$ Submerged Volume $V_{\text{submerged}}=Ah$ (where h is the submerged height) $\Rightarrow$ $\rho_{b}(AH)=\rho_{l}(Ah) \Rightarrow h=(\frac{\rho_{b}}{\rho_{l}})H$ Putting the given values, $\rho_{b}=600kg/m^{3},\rho_{l}=900kg/m^{3}\text{and}H=8.0cm$ $\Rightarrow$ $h=(\frac{600}{900}) \times 8.0cm \approx 5.33cm$ Therefore, the height of the submerged part of the block is approximately 5.3 cm. Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
When an object floats in a liquid, the weight of the object is exactly balanced by the buoyant force (up thrust) exerted by the liquid.

Weight of block is $=W=m \cdot g=(\rho_{b} \times V_{\text{total}}) \times g$

Buoyant force ( $F_{B}$ ) acting on a submerged body is equal to the weight of displaced liquid,

$F_{B}=(\rho_{1}V_{\text{submerged}}) \times g$

For flotation :

$W=F_{B}$

$\rho_{b}V_{\text{total}}g=\rho_{l}V_{\text{submerged}}g$

For a cubical block with a uniform cross-sectional area (A):

Total Volume $=V_{\text{total}}=AH$

Submerged Volume $V_{\text{submerged}}=Ah$ (where h is the submerged height)

$\Rightarrow$ $\rho_{b}(AH)=\rho_{l}(Ah) \Rightarrow h=(\frac{\rho_{b}}{\rho_{l}})H$

Putting the given values,

$\rho_{b}=600kg/m^{3},\rho_{l}=900kg/m^{3}\text{and}H=8.0cm$

$\Rightarrow$ $h=(\frac{600}{900}) \times 8.0cm \approx 5.33cm$

Therefore, the height of the submerged part of the block is approximately 5.3 cm.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: When a part of a straight capillary tube is placed vertically in a liquid, the liquid raises upto certain height $ℎ$ . If the inner radius of the capillary tube, density of the liquid and surface tension of the liquid decrease by $1%$ each, then the height of the liquid in the tube will change by $____$ $%$ .
questions.question_html: When a part of a straight capillary tube is placed vertically in a liquid, the liquid raises upto certain height $ℎ$ . If the inner radius of the capillary tube, density of the liquid and surface tension of the liquid decrease by $1%$ each, then the height of the liquid in the tube will change by $____$ $%$ .
questions.explanation_text: The height (h) to which a liquid rises in a capillary tube is given by: $h=\frac{2Scos\theta}{r\rho g}$ Where : S is the surface tension of the liquid. $\theta$ is the angle of contact. $r$ is the inner radius of the capillary tube. $\rho$ is the density of the liquid. $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. Assuming the angle of contact ( θ) and gravity ( $g$ ) remain constant, the height $ℎ$ depends on variables $S,r$ , and $\rho$ as, $ℎ∝\frac{S}{r\rho}$ Taking the natural logarithm of both sides : $ln(ℎ)=ln(S)-ln(r)-ln(\rho)+\text{constant}$ Differentiating this equation, $\frac{\Delta h}{h}=\frac{\Delta S}{S}-\frac{\Delta r}{r}-\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}$ So, the percentage change in height is, $%\Delta h=%\Delta S-%\Delta r-%\Delta\rho$ It is given that all three quantities (radius, density, and surface tension) decrease by $1%$ . Therefore, their percentage changes are negative : Change in surface tension, $%\Delta S=-1%$ Change in inner radius, $%\Delta r=-1%$ Change in density, $%\Delta\rho=-1%$ Substituting these values into our percentage change equation : $%\Delta h=(-1%)-(-1%)-(-1%)$ $\Rightarrow$ $%\Deltaℎ=-1%+1%+1%=1%$ The positive sign indicates that the height of the liquid in the tube will increase by $1%$ . Hence, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
The height (h) to which a liquid rises in a capillary tube is given by:

$h=\frac{2Scos\theta}{r\rho g}$

Where :

  • S is the surface tension of the liquid.

  • $\theta$ is the angle of contact.

  • $r$ is the inner radius of the capillary tube.

  • $\rho$ is the density of the liquid.

  • $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Assuming the angle of contact ( θ) and gravity ( $g$ ) remain constant, the height $ℎ$ depends on variables $S,r$ , and $\rho$ as,

$ℎ∝\frac{S}{r\rho}$

Taking the natural logarithm of both sides :

$ln(ℎ)=ln(S)-ln(r)-ln(\rho)+\text{constant}$

Differentiating this equation,

$\frac{\Delta h}{h}=\frac{\Delta S}{S}-\frac{\Delta r}{r}-\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}$

So, the percentage change in height is,

$%\Delta h=%\Delta S-%\Delta r-%\Delta\rho$

It is given that all three quantities (radius, density, and surface tension) decrease by $1%$ . Therefore, their percentage changes are negative :

  • Change in surface tension, $%\Delta S=-1%$

  • Change in inner radius, $%\Delta r=-1%$

  • Change in density, $%\Delta\rho=-1%$

Substituting these values into our percentage change equation :

$%\Delta h=(-1%)-(-1%)-(-1%)$

$\Rightarrow$ $%\Deltaℎ=-1%+1%+1%=1%$

The positive sign indicates that the height of the liquid in the tube will increase by $1%$ . Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: Water flows through a horizontal tube as shown in the figure. The difference in height between the water columns in vertical tubes is 5 cm and the area of cross-sections at $A$ and $B$ are $6cm^{2}$ and $3cm^{2}$ respectively. The rate of flow will be $____$ $cm^{3}/s$ . (take $g=10m/s^{2}$ )
questions.question_html: Water flows through a horizontal tube as shown in the figure. The difference in height between the water columns in vertical tubes is 5 cm and the area of cross-sections at $A$ and $B$ are $6cm^{2}$ and $3cm^{2}$ respectively. The rate of flow will be $____$ $cm^{3}/s$ . (take $g=10m/s^{2}$ )
questions.explanation_text: Applying the equation of continuity The rate of flow ( Q ) is constant throughout the tube. $Q=A_{1}v_{1}=A_{2}v_{2}$ Where : $A_{1}=$ cross-section area at $A,A_{1}=6cm^{2}$ $A_{2}=$ cross-section area at $B,A_{2}=3cm^{2}$ $V_{1},V_{2}$ are velocities at A and B . $6v_{1}=3v_{2} \Rightarrow v_{2}=2v_{1}$ Applying Bernoulli's principle between two points, $P_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{1}^{2}+\rho gℎ_{1}=P_{2}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{2}^{2}$ For a horizontal tube, the height is the same, $h_{1}=h_{2}$ $P_{1}-P_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\rho(v_{2}^{2}-v_{1}^{2})$ The pressure difference ( $P_{1}-P_{2}$ ) is measured by the difference in the heights of the water columns ( $ℎ$ ) : $P_{1}-P_{2}=\rho gh$ From relations (ii) and (iii), $\rho gℎ=\frac{1}{2}\rho(v_{2}^{2}-v_{1}^{2})$ $\Rightarrow$ $2gℎ=v_{2}^{2}-v_{1}^{2}$ Substituting $v_{2}=2v_{1}$ from relation (i) : $2gℎ=(2v_{1})^{2}-v_{1}^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $2gℎ=4v_{1}^{2}-v_{1}^{2}=3v_{1}^{2}$ $\Rightarrow v_{1}=\sqrt{2gℎ/3}$ The given values are, $g=10m/s^{2}=1000cm/s^{2}$ $h=5cm$ Putting the values, $v_{1}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1000 \times 5}{3}}=\sqrt{\frac{10000}{3}}=\frac{100}{\sqrt{3}}cm/s$ So, the rate of flow (Q), $Q=A_{1} \cdot v_{1}$ $\Rightarrow$ $Q=6 \cdot \frac{100}{\sqrt{3}}=2 \times \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \times \frac{100}{\sqrt{3}}=200\sqrt{3}cm^{3}/s$ Therefore, the rate of flow of water through the horizontal tube is $200\sqrt{3}cm^{3}/s$ . Hence, the correct option is (D).
questions.explanation_html:
Applying the equation of continuity

The rate of flow ( Q ) is constant throughout the tube.

$Q=A_{1}v_{1}=A_{2}v_{2}$

Where :

  • $A_{1}=$ cross-section area at $A,A_{1}=6cm^{2}$

  • $A_{2}=$ cross-section area at $B,A_{2}=3cm^{2}$

  • $V_{1},V_{2}$ are velocities at A and B .

$6v_{1}=3v_{2} \Rightarrow v_{2}=2v_{1}$

Applying Bernoulli's principle between two points,

$P_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{1}^{2}+\rho gℎ_{1}=P_{2}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{2}^{2}$

For a horizontal tube, the height is the same, $h_{1}=h_{2}$

$P_{1}-P_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\rho(v_{2}^{2}-v_{1}^{2})$

The pressure difference ( $P_{1}-P_{2}$ ) is measured by the difference in the heights of the water columns ( $ℎ$ ) :

$P_{1}-P_{2}=\rho gh$

From relations (ii) and (iii),

$\rho gℎ=\frac{1}{2}\rho(v_{2}^{2}-v_{1}^{2})$

$\Rightarrow$ $2gℎ=v_{2}^{2}-v_{1}^{2}$

Substituting $v_{2}=2v_{1}$ from relation (i) :

$2gℎ=(2v_{1})^{2}-v_{1}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $2gℎ=4v_{1}^{2}-v_{1}^{2}=3v_{1}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow v_{1}=\sqrt{2gℎ/3}$

The given values are,

  • $g=10m/s^{2}=1000cm/s^{2}$

  • $h=5cm$

Putting the values,

$v_{1}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1000 \times 5}{3}}=\sqrt{\frac{10000}{3}}=\frac{100}{\sqrt{3}}cm/s$

So, the rate of flow (Q),

$Q=A_{1} \cdot v_{1}$

$\Rightarrow$ $Q=6 \cdot \frac{100}{\sqrt{3}}=2 \times \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \times \frac{100}{\sqrt{3}}=200\sqrt{3}cm^{3}/s$

Therefore, the rate of flow of water through the horizontal tube is $200\sqrt{3}cm^{3}/s$ .

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.question_text: A uniform wire of length $l$ of weight $w$ is suspended from the roof with a weight of $W$ at the other end. The stress in the wire at $\frac{l}{3}$ distance from the top is $(\frac{W}{A}+\frac{2}{\gamma}\frac{w}{A})$ , where $A$ is the cross sectional area of the wire. The value of $\gamma$ is ________.
questions.question_html: A uniform wire of length $l$ of weight $w$ is suspended from the roof with a weight of $W$ at the other end. The stress in the wire at $\frac{l}{3}$ distance from the top is $(\frac{W}{A}+\frac{2}{\gamma}\frac{w}{A})$ , where $A$ is the cross sectional area of the wire. The value of $\gamma$ is ________.
questions.explanation_text: Stress is force (tension) per unit cross-sectional area. In a suspended wire with mass, the tension varies along its length because the wire must support the weight of the portion below it. We need the stress at a distance $x=\frac{1}{3}$ from the top. This means the point is $l-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{21}{3}$ distance from the bottom. The total tension $T$ at this point must support the load weight $W$ attached to the bottom and weight of the portion of the wire hanging below this point $(w^{'})$ . Since the wire is uniform, weight per unit length is $\lambda=\frac{w}{l}$ . The length of the wire below the point is $L_{\text{below}}=\frac{2l}{3}$ . $w^{'}=\lambda \times L_{\text{below}}=(\frac{W}{l})(\frac{2l}{3})=\frac{2w}{3}$ So, total tension $T$ at the point: $T=W+w^{'}=W+\frac{2w}{3}$ So, the stress in wire is, $\sigma=\frac{T}{A}=\frac{W+\frac{2w}{3}}{A}$ $\sigma=\frac{W}{A}+\frac{2w}{3A}=(\frac{W}{A}+\frac{2w}{\gamma A})$ $\Rightarrow \frac{2}{3}=\frac{2}{\gamma}$ $\gamma=3$ Therefore, the value of $\gamma$ is $3$ . Thus, the correct answer is $3$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Stress is force (tension) per unit cross-sectional area.

In a suspended wire with mass, the tension varies along its length because the wire must support the weight of the portion below it.

We need the stress at a distance $x=\frac{1}{3}$ from the top. This means the point is $l-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{21}{3}$ distance from the bottom.

The total tension $T$ at this point must support the load weight $W$ attached to the bottom and weight of the portion

of the wire hanging below this point $(w^{'})$ .

Since the wire is uniform, weight per unit length is $\lambda=\frac{w}{l}$ .

The length of the wire below the point is $L_{\text{below}}=\frac{2l}{3}$ .

$w^{'}=\lambda \times L_{\text{below}}=(\frac{W}{l})(\frac{2l}{3})=\frac{2w}{3}$

So, total tension $T$ at the point:

$T=W+w^{'}=W+\frac{2w}{3}$

So, the stress in wire is,

$\sigma=\frac{T}{A}=\frac{W+\frac{2w}{3}}{A}$

$\sigma=\frac{W}{A}+\frac{2w}{3A}=(\frac{W}{A}+\frac{2w}{\gamma A})$

$\Rightarrow \frac{2}{3}=\frac{2}{\gamma}$

$\gamma=3$

Therefore, the value of $\gamma$ is $3$ . Thus, the correct answer is $3$ .

questions.question_text: A ball of radius $r$ and density $\rho$ dropped through a viscous liquid of density $\sigma$ and viscosity $\eta$ attains its terminal velocity at time $t$ , given by $t=A\rho^{a}r^{b}\eta^{c}\sigma^{d}$ , where $A$ is a constant and $a,b,c$ and $d$ are integers. The value of $\frac{b+c}{a+d}$ is $____$ .
questions.question_html: A ball of radius $r$ and density $\rho$ dropped through a viscous liquid of density $\sigma$ and viscosity $\eta$ attains its terminal velocity at time $t$ , given by $t=A\rho^{a}r^{b}\eta^{c}\sigma^{d}$ , where $A$ is a constant and $a,b,c$ and $d$ are integers. The value of $\frac{b+c}{a+d}$ is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: Dimensions of Each Quantity We first write the dimensions of every symbol in the formula. Time $[t]=[M^{0}L^{0}T^{1}]$ Density $[\rho]=[\sigma]=[\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}}]=[ML^{-3}]$ Radius $[r]=[L]$ From Stokes' Law ( $F=6\pi\eta$ rv), we have $\eta=$ F/rv. Using Stokes’ law, $\eta$ depends on force, radius, and velocity, so its dimensions come from $F$ , $r$ , and $v$ . Dimension $=[MLT^{-2}][L^{-1}][L^{-1}T]=[ML^{-1}T^{-1}]$ Constant (A) is dimensionless According to the given formula $t=A\rho^{a}r^{b}\eta^{c}\sigma^{d}$ : $[T]=[ML^{-3}]^{a}[L]^{b}[ML^{-1}T^{-1}]^{c}[ML^{-3}]^{d}$ $\Rightarrow$ $[M^{0}L^{0}T^{1}]=[M^{a+c+d}][L^{-3a+b-c-3d}][T^{-c}]$ Comparing the exponents for $M,L$ , and T on both sides : For $T:-c=1 \Rightarrow c=-1$ For $M:a+c+d=0 \Rightarrow a-1+d=0 \Rightarrow a+d=1$ For $L:-3a+b-c-3d=0$ Substituting $c=-1$ : $-3a+b+1-3d=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $b+1-3(a+d)=0$ Substituting $(a+d)=1$ $b+1-3(1)=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $b-2=0 \Rightarrow b=2$ We need to find the value of $\frac{b+c}{a+d}$ : $\frac{b+c}{a+d}=\frac{2+(-1)}{1}=1$ Therefore, the correct answer is $𝟏$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Dimensions of Each Quantity

We first write the dimensions of every symbol in the formula.

Time $[t]=[M^{0}L^{0}T^{1}]$

Density $[\rho]=[\sigma]=[\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}}]=[ML^{-3}]$

Radius $[r]=[L]$

From Stokes' Law ( $F=6\pi\eta$ rv), we have $\eta=$ F/rv.

Using Stokes’ law, $\eta$ depends on force, radius, and velocity, so its dimensions come from $F$ , $r$ , and $v$ .

Dimension $=[MLT^{-2}][L^{-1}][L^{-1}T]=[ML^{-1}T^{-1}]$

Constant (A) is dimensionless

According to the given formula $t=A\rho^{a}r^{b}\eta^{c}\sigma^{d}$ :

$[T]=[ML^{-3}]^{a}[L]^{b}[ML^{-1}T^{-1}]^{c}[ML^{-3}]^{d}$

$\Rightarrow$ $[M^{0}L^{0}T^{1}]=[M^{a+c+d}][L^{-3a+b-c-3d}][T^{-c}]$

Comparing the exponents for $M,L$ , and T on both sides :

For $T:-c=1 \Rightarrow c=-1$

For $M:a+c+d=0 \Rightarrow a-1+d=0 \Rightarrow a+d=1$

For $L:-3a+b-c-3d=0$

Substituting $c=-1$ :

$-3a+b+1-3d=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $b+1-3(a+d)=0$

Substituting $(a+d)=1$

$b+1-3(1)=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $b-2=0 \Rightarrow b=2$

We need to find the value of $\frac{b+c}{a+d}$ :

$\frac{b+c}{a+d}=\frac{2+(-1)}{1}=1$

Therefore, the correct answer is $𝟏$ .

questions.question_text: Figure represents the extension $(\Delta l)$ of a wire of length 1 meter, suspended from the ceiling of the room at one end with a load $W$ connected to the other end. If the cross-sectional area of the wire is $10^{-5}m^{2}$ then the Young's modulus of the wire is $____$ $N/m^{2}$ .
questions.question_html: Figure represents the extension $(\Delta l)$ of a wire of length 1 meter, suspended from the ceiling of the room at one end with a load $W$ connected to the other end. If the cross-sectional area of the wire is $10^{-5}m^{2}$ then the Young's modulus of the wire is $____$ $N/m^{2}$ .
questions.explanation_text: Young's Modulus (Y) is defined as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the elastic limit. Stress ( $\sigma$ ) is force (W) per unit cross-sectional area (A). $\sigma=\frac{W}{A}$ Strain $(\epsilon)$ is extension $(\Delta l)$ per unit original length $(L)$ . $\epsilon=\frac{\Delta l}{L}$ Thus, Young's Modulus is : $Y=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}=\frac{W/A}{\Delta l/L}$ $Y=\frac{WL}{A\Delta l}$ The original length is $L=1m$ The cross-sectional area is $A=10^{-5}m^{2}$ From the graph, we need a pair of values for W and $\Delta l$ . Let's take $W=20N$ and the corresponding extension $\Delta l=2 \times 10^{-4}m$ . Substituting the values in the expression for Young's modulus; $Y=\frac{20 \times 1}{10^{-5} \times (2 \times 10^{-4})}$ $\Rightarrow$ $Y=\frac{20}{2 \times 10^{-9}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $Y=10 \times 10^{9}$ $Y=1.0 \times 10^{10}N/m^{2}$ Therefore, the Young's modulus of the wire is $1.0 \times 10^{10}N/m^{2}$ . Thus, the correct option is (C).
questions.explanation_html:
Young's Modulus (Y) is defined as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the elastic limit.

Stress ( $\sigma$ ) is force (W) per unit cross-sectional area (A).

$\sigma=\frac{W}{A}$

Strain $(\epsilon)$ is extension $(\Delta l)$ per unit original length $(L)$ .

$\epsilon=\frac{\Delta l}{L}$

Thus, Young's Modulus is :

$Y=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}=\frac{W/A}{\Delta l/L}$

$Y=\frac{WL}{A\Delta l}$

The original length is $L=1m$

The cross-sectional area is $A=10^{-5}m^{2}$

From the graph, we need a pair of values for W and $\Delta l$ .

Let's take $W=20N$ and the corresponding extension $\Delta l=2 \times 10^{-4}m$ .

Substituting the values in the expression for Young's modulus;

$Y=\frac{20 \times 1}{10^{-5} \times (2 \times 10^{-4})}$

$\Rightarrow$ $Y=\frac{20}{2 \times 10^{-9}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $Y=10 \times 10^{9}$

$Y=1.0 \times 10^{10}N/m^{2}$

Therefore, the Young's modulus of the wire is $1.0 \times 10^{10}N/m^{2}$ . Thus, the correct option is (C).

questions.question_text: Eight mercury drops, each of radius $r$ , coalesce to form a bigger drop. The surface energy released in this process is $____$ - ( $S$ is the surface tension of mercury).
questions.question_html: Eight mercury drops, each of radius $r$ , coalesce to form a bigger drop. The surface energy released in this process is $____$ - ( $S$ is the surface tension of mercury).
questions.explanation_text: When 8 small drops of radius $r$ combine to form one large drop of radius $R$ , the total volume remains constant. Volume of 8 small drops $=$ Volume of 1 large drop $8 \times (\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3})=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $8r^{3}=R^{3}$ $\Rightarrow R=2r$ The surface energy of a single drop is $E=SA$ where $S$ is the surface tension and $A$ is the surface area. Total initial area for 8 drops $=8 \times (4\pi r^{2})=32\pi r^{2}$ . So, total initial surface energy is $U_{i}=32\pi r^{2}S$ The final drop has radius $R=2r$ . So, final surface area $=4\pi R^{2}=4\pi(2r)^{2}=4\pi(4r^{2})=16\pi r^{2}$ . So, the final surface energy is $U_{f}=16\pi r^{2}S$ The energy released is the decrease in surface energy : $\Delta U=U_{i}-U_{f}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta U=32\pi r^{2}S-16\pi r^{2}S$ $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta U=16\pi r^{2}S$ Therefore, the surface energy released in this process is $16\pi r^{2}S$ . Hence, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
When 8 small drops of radius $r$ combine to form one large drop of radius $R$ , the total volume remains constant.

Volume of 8 small drops $=$ Volume of 1 large drop

$8 \times (\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3})=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $8r^{3}=R^{3}$

$\Rightarrow R=2r$

The surface energy of a single drop is $E=SA$ where $S$ is the surface tension and $A$ is the surface area.

Total initial area for 8 drops $=8 \times (4\pi r^{2})=32\pi r^{2}$ .

So, total initial surface energy is $U_{i}=32\pi r^{2}S$

The final drop has radius $R=2r$ .

So, final surface area $=4\pi R^{2}=4\pi(2r)^{2}=4\pi(4r^{2})=16\pi r^{2}$ .

So, the final surface energy is $U_{f}=16\pi r^{2}S$

The energy released is the decrease in surface energy :

$\Delta U=U_{i}-U_{f}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta U=32\pi r^{2}S-16\pi r^{2}S$

$\Rightarrow$ $\Delta U=16\pi r^{2}S$

Therefore, the surface energy released in this process is $16\pi r^{2}S$ .

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: A water spray gun is attached to a hose of cross sectional area $30cm^{2}$ . The gun comprises of 10 perforations each of cross sectional area of $15mm^{2}$ . If the water flows in the hose with the speed of $50cm/s$ , calculate the speed at which the water flows out from each perforation. (Neglect any edge effects)
questions.question_html: A water spray gun is attached to a hose of cross sectional area $30cm^{2}$ . The gun comprises of 10 perforations each of cross sectional area of $15mm^{2}$ . If the water flows in the hose with the speed of $50cm/s$ , calculate the speed at which the water flows out from each perforation. (Neglect any edge effects)
questions.explanation_text: For an incompressible fluid, the volume of fluid entering a pipe per unit time must equal the volume of fluid leaving the pipe per unit time. Volume Flow Rate (In) = Volume Flow Rate (Out) $A_{1}v_{1}=A_{2}v_{2}$ Where A is the area and v is the velocity of the fluid. The area of hose is $A_{1}=30cm^{2}=30 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$ . The speed in hose is $v_{1}=50cm/s=0.5m/s$ . Number of perforations is $n=10$ . The area of one perforation is $a=15mm^{2}=15 \times (10^{-3}m)^{2}=15 \times 10^{-6}m^{2}$ So, total area of exit is, $A_{2}=n \times a=10 \times 15 \times 10^{-6}=150 \times 10^{-6}m^{2}$ Using the equation of continuity: $A_{1}v_{1}=A_{2}v_{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_{2}=\frac{A_{1}v_{1}}{A_{2}}$ Substituting the values : $v_{2}=\frac{(30 \times 10^{-4}) \times 0.5}{150 \times 10^{-6}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_{2}=\frac{15 \times 10^{-4}}{150 \times 10^{-6}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_{2}=10m/s$ Therefore, the speed at which the water flows out from each perforation is $10m/s$ . Thus, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
For an incompressible fluid, the volume of fluid entering a pipe per unit time must equal the volume of fluid leaving the pipe per unit time.

Volume Flow Rate (In) = Volume Flow Rate (Out)

$A_{1}v_{1}=A_{2}v_{2}$

Where A is the area and v is the velocity of the fluid.

The area of hose is $A_{1}=30cm^{2}=30 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$ .

The speed in hose is $v_{1}=50cm/s=0.5m/s$ .

Number of perforations is $n=10$ .

The area of one perforation is $a=15mm^{2}=15 \times (10^{-3}m)^{2}=15 \times 10^{-6}m^{2}$

So, total area of exit is, $A_{2}=n \times a=10 \times 15 \times 10^{-6}=150 \times 10^{-6}m^{2}$

Using the equation of continuity:

$A_{1}v_{1}=A_{2}v_{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $v_{2}=\frac{A_{1}v_{1}}{A_{2}}$

Substituting the values :

$v_{2}=\frac{(30 \times 10^{-4}) \times 0.5}{150 \times 10^{-6}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $v_{2}=\frac{15 \times 10^{-4}}{150 \times 10^{-6}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $v_{2}=10m/s$

Therefore, the speed at which the water flows out from each perforation is $10m/s$ .

Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: If an air bubble of diameter 2 mm rises steadily through a liquid of density 2000 kg/m 3 at a rate of 0.5 cm/s, then the coefficient of viscosity of liquid is ______ Poise. (Take g = 10 m/s 2 )
questions.question_html: If an air bubble of diameter 2 mm rises steadily through a liquid of density 2000 kg/m3 at a rate of 0.5 cm/s, then the coefficient of viscosity of liquid is ______ Poise. (Take g = 10 m/s2)
questions.explanation_text: When the bubble rises steadily, the net force is zero. The forces involved are : Buoyant force $(F_{B})$ acting upwards: $F_{B}=V\sigma g$ , where $\sigma$ is liquid density and V is the volume of the bubble. Weight ( $F_{g}$ ) acting downwards: $W=V\rho g$ , where $\rho$ is air density. Viscous drag $(F_{v})$ acting downwards (opposing motion) : $F_{v}=6\pi\eta rv$ , where $\eta$ is the viscosity of liquid, r is the radius of body and v is the speed. As the bubble is rising steadily, so the net force acting on it should be zero. Equating the forces : $F_{B}=W+F_{v}$ $\Rightarrow$ $V\sigma g=V\rho g+6\pi\eta rv$ Since the density of air ( $\rho$ ) is much smaller than the density of the liquid ( $\sigma=2000kg/m^{3}$ ), we can neglect W : $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\sigma g=6\pi\eta rv$ $\Rightarrow$ $\eta=\frac{2r^{2}\sigma g}{9v}$ The radius of bubble is $r=\frac{2mm}{2}=1mm=10^{-3}m$ The density of liquid is $\sigma=2000kg/m^{3}$ The constant speed of rise of bubble is $v=0.5cm/s=0.005m/s=5 \times 10^{-3}m/s$ And the acceleration due to gravity is $g=10m/s^{2}$ Putting the values, $\eta=\frac{2 \times (10^{-3})^{2} \times 2000 \times 10}{9 \times 5 \times 10^{-3}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\eta=\frac{2 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 \times 10^{4}}{45 \times 10^{-3}}=\frac{4 \times 10^{-2}}{45 \times 10^{-3}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\eta=\frac{40}{45} \approx 0.888Pa \cdot s$ As Pa.s is the SI unit of viscosity and the required value is in CGS unit, Poise; $1Pa \cdot s=10\text{Poise} \Rightarrow \eta=0.888 \times 10=8.88\text{Poise}$ Therefore, the correct option is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
When the bubble rises steadily, the net force is zero. The forces involved are :

Buoyant force $(F_{B})$ acting upwards: $F_{B}=V\sigma g$ , where $\sigma$ is liquid density and V is the volume of the bubble.

Weight ( $F_{g}$ ) acting downwards: $W=V\rho g$ , where $\rho$ is air density.

Viscous drag $(F_{v})$ acting downwards (opposing motion) :

$F_{v}=6\pi\eta rv$ , where $\eta$ is the viscosity of liquid, r is the radius of body and v is the speed.

As the bubble is rising steadily, so the net force acting on it should be zero.

Equating the forces :

$F_{B}=W+F_{v}$

$\Rightarrow$ $V\sigma g=V\rho g+6\pi\eta rv$

Since the density of air ( $\rho$ ) is much smaller than the density of the liquid ( $\sigma=2000kg/m^{3}$ ), we can neglect W :

$\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\sigma g=6\pi\eta rv$

$\Rightarrow$ $\eta=\frac{2r^{2}\sigma g}{9v}$

The radius of bubble is $r=\frac{2mm}{2}=1mm=10^{-3}m$

The density of liquid is $\sigma=2000kg/m^{3}$

The constant speed of rise of bubble is $v=0.5cm/s=0.005m/s=5 \times 10^{-3}m/s$

And the acceleration due to gravity is $g=10m/s^{2}$

Putting the values,

$\eta=\frac{2 \times (10^{-3})^{2} \times 2000 \times 10}{9 \times 5 \times 10^{-3}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\eta=\frac{2 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 \times 10^{4}}{45 \times 10^{-3}}=\frac{4 \times 10^{-2}}{45 \times 10^{-3}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\eta=\frac{40}{45} \approx 0.888Pa \cdot s$

As Pa.s is the SI unit of viscosity and the required value is in CGS unit, Poise;

$1Pa \cdot s=10\text{Poise} \Rightarrow \eta=0.888 \times 10=8.88\text{Poise}$

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

questions.question_text: A brass wire of length 2 m and radius 1 mm at $27^{\circ}C$ is held taut between two rigid supports. Initially it was cooled to a temperature of $-43^{\circ}C$ creating a tension $T$ in the wire. The temperature to which the wire has to be cooled in order to increase the tension in it to $1.4T$ , is $____$ $^{\circ}C$ .
questions.question_html: A brass wire of length 2 m and radius 1 mm at $27^{\circ}C$ is held taut between two rigid supports. Initially it was cooled to a temperature of $-43^{\circ}C$ creating a tension $T$ in the wire. The temperature to which the wire has to be cooled in order to increase the tension in it to $1.4T$ , is $____$ $^{\circ}C$ .
questions.explanation_text: A metal rod of original length $L$ that is free to move. If we heat this rod by a temperature difference $\Delta T$ , it will naturally expand. The change in length ( $\Delta L$ ) is given by the law of linear thermal expansion : $\Delta L=L \cdot \alpha \cdot \Delta T$ Where $\alpha=$ Coefficient of Linear Expansion When a wire fixed at both ends is cooled, it contracts. Since the supports are rigid, they prevent this contraction, creating a tension in the wire. $\text{Strain}\epsilon=\frac{\Delta L}{L}=\alpha\Delta T$ According to Hooke's Law, Stress is proportional to Strain within the elastic limit. The constant of proportionality is Young's Modulus (Y). $Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}$ $\Rightarrow$ Stress $(\sigma)=Y \times$ Strain $\sigma=Y \cdot (\alpha\Delta T)$ Stress is defined as Force (F) per unit Area (A). $\text{Stress}=\frac{F}{A}=Y \cdot (\alpha\Delta T)$ $\Rightarrow$ $F=(Y\alpha\Delta T) \times A$ $\Rightarrow F∝\Delta T \Rightarrow \frac{F_{1}}{F_{2}}=\frac{\Delta T_{1}}{\Delta T_{2}}$ Initial Temperature $=t_{0}=27^{\circ}C$ Final Temperature $=t_{1}=-43^{\circ}C$ $\Delta T_{1}=27-(-43)=70^{\circ}C$ Initial tension in the wire is, $F_{1}=T$ Final tension in the wire is $F_{2}=1.4T$ Let the new final temperature be $t_{2}$ . $\Delta T_{2}=27-t_{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{F_{2}}{F_{1}}=\frac{1.4T}{T}=\frac{27-t_{2}}{70}$ $\Rightarrow$ $1.4=\frac{27-t_{2}}{70}$ $\Rightarrow$ $27-t_{2}=1.4 \times 70$ $\Rightarrow$ $27-t_{2}=98$ $\Rightarrow$ $t_{2}=27-98$ $\Rightarrow$ $t_{2}=-71^{\circ}C$
questions.explanation_html:
A metal rod of original length $L$ that is free to move. If we heat this rod by a temperature difference $\Delta T$ , it will naturally expand.

The change in length ( $\Delta L$ ) is given by the law of linear thermal expansion :

$\Delta L=L \cdot \alpha \cdot \Delta T$

Where $\alpha=$ Coefficient of Linear Expansion

When a wire fixed at both ends is cooled, it contracts. Since the supports are rigid, they prevent this contraction, creating a tension in the wire.

$\text{Strain}\epsilon=\frac{\Delta L}{L}=\alpha\Delta T$

According to Hooke's Law, Stress is proportional to Strain within the elastic limit. The constant of proportionality is Young's Modulus (Y).

$Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}$

$\Rightarrow$ Stress $(\sigma)=Y \times$ Strain

$\sigma=Y \cdot (\alpha\Delta T)$

Stress is defined as Force (F) per unit Area (A).

$\text{Stress}=\frac{F}{A}=Y \cdot (\alpha\Delta T)$

$\Rightarrow$ $F=(Y\alpha\Delta T) \times A$

$\Rightarrow F∝\Delta T \Rightarrow \frac{F_{1}}{F_{2}}=\frac{\Delta T_{1}}{\Delta T_{2}}$

Initial Temperature $=t_{0}=27^{\circ}C$

Final Temperature $=t_{1}=-43^{\circ}C$

$\Delta T_{1}=27-(-43)=70^{\circ}C$

Initial tension in the wire is, $F_{1}=T$

Final tension in the wire is $F_{2}=1.4T$

Let the new final temperature be $t_{2}$ .

$\Delta T_{2}=27-t_{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{F_{2}}{F_{1}}=\frac{1.4T}{T}=\frac{27-t_{2}}{70}$

$\Rightarrow$ $1.4=\frac{27-t_{2}}{70}$

$\Rightarrow$ $27-t_{2}=1.4 \times 70$

$\Rightarrow$ $27-t_{2}=98$

$\Rightarrow$ $t_{2}=27-98$

$\Rightarrow$ $t_{2}=-71^{\circ}C$

questions.question_text: Given below are two statements : Statement I : Pressure of a fluid is exerted only on a solid surface in contact as the fluid-pressure does not exist everywhere in a still fluid. Statement II : Excess potential energy of the molecules on the surface of a liquid, when compared to interior, results in surface tension. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
questions.question_html:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : Pressure of a fluid is exerted only on a solid surface in contact as the fluid-pressure does not exist everywhere in a still fluid.

Statement II : Excess potential energy of the molecules on the surface of a liquid, when compared to interior, results in surface tension.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.label: A
options.text: Statement I is false but Statement II is true
options.html: Statement I is false but Statement II is true

options.label: B
options.text: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
options.html: Statement I is true but Statement II is false

options.label: C
options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
options.html: Both Statement I and Statement II are false

options.label: D
options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
options.html: Both Statement I and Statement II are true

questions.explanation_text: Statement I Consider an imaginary cube of water out of still water in a container, This tiny cube has mass, so gravity is pulling it down. If nothing were pushing back up against it, it would fall to the bottom. However, the fluid is still (in static equilibrium). This means the net force on our imaginary cube must be zero. The water below our imaginary cube must be pushing up on it to counteract gravity. Similarly, the water on the sides is pushing inward to keep it from spreading. This pushing force per unit area is exactly what pressure is. Therefore, the surrounding fluid exerts pressure on our imaginary surface inside the bulk of the liquid. Pressure is a scalar property that exists at every single point within a fluid, not just where it touches a solid container. Therefore, the statement I is false. Statement II A molecule deep in the interior is completely surrounded by other identical molecules on all sides. The attractive forces pull it equally in every direction. The net force on an interior molecule is zero. A molecule on the surface has molecules next to it and below it, but practically none above it. Because it is missing half of its neighbours, there is a net inward force pulling the surface molecule down into the bulk of the liquid. Now, if it is to bring an interior molecule up to the surface to create more surface area. It has to be pulled against that net inward force. And whenever an object moves against an opposing force by external force, then work must be done. By the Work-Energy Theorem, the work is stored as Potential Energy. Therefore, molecules on the surface possess higher potential energy than those in the bulk interior. Any system always prefers the lowest possible energy state. Because having surface molecules costs extra energy, a liquid will naturally try to minimize the number of molecules on its surface. It does this by minimizing its overall surface area. This macroscopic tendency of a liquid surface to shrink and act like a stretched elastic membrane is exactly what we call surface tension. Therefore, the statement II is true. So, statement I is false, and Statement II is true. Hence, the correct option is (A).
questions.explanation_html:
Statement I

Consider an imaginary cube of water out of still water in a container,

This tiny cube has mass, so gravity is pulling it down. If nothing were pushing back up against it, it would fall to the bottom. However, the fluid is still (in static equilibrium). This means the net force on our imaginary cube must be zero.

The water below our imaginary cube must be pushing up on it to counteract gravity. Similarly, the water on the sides is pushing inward to keep it from spreading.

This pushing force per unit area is exactly what pressure is. Therefore, the surrounding fluid exerts pressure on our imaginary surface inside the bulk of the liquid. Pressure is a scalar property that exists at every single point within a fluid, not just where it touches a solid container.

Therefore, the statement I is false.

Statement II

A molecule deep in the interior is completely surrounded by other identical molecules on all sides. The attractive forces pull it equally in every direction. The net force on an interior molecule is zero.

A molecule on the surface has molecules next to it and below it, but practically none above it. Because it is missing half of its neighbours, there is a net inward force pulling the surface molecule down into the bulk of the liquid.

Now, if it is to bring an interior molecule up to the surface to create more surface area. It has to be pulled against that net inward force. And whenever an object moves against an opposing force by external force, then work must be done.

By the Work-Energy Theorem, the work is stored as Potential Energy. Therefore, molecules on the surface possess higher potential energy than those in the bulk interior.

Any system always prefers the lowest possible energy state. Because having surface molecules costs extra energy, a liquid will naturally try to minimize the number of molecules on its surface. It does this by minimizing its overall surface area. This macroscopic tendency of a liquid surface to shrink and act like a stretched elastic membrane is exactly what we call surface tension.

Therefore, the statement II is true.

So, statement I is false, and Statement II is true.

Hence, the correct option is (A).
