  • $\rho_{f}$ is the density of the fluid (the solution), and
  • $\eta$ is the coefficient of viscosity of the fluid.

Since we are neglecting the density of the air bubble, the formula simplifies to:

$v=\frac{2}{9}\frac{r^{2}g\rho_{f}}{\eta}$ .

Rearranging for $\eta$ , we get:

Given that $r=\frac{6\text{mm}}{2}=3\text{mm}=3 \times 10^{-3}\text{m}$ , $g=10\text{ms}^{-2}$ , $\rho_{f}=1750\text{kg/m}^{3}$ , and $v=0.35\text{cm/s}=0.35 \times 10^{-2}\text{m/s}$ , we can substitute these values into the formula to find $\eta$ :

$\eta=\frac{2}{9}\frac{(3 \times 10^{-3})^{2} \times 10 \times 1750}{0.35 \times 10^{-2}}=10\text{Pas}$ .

Therefore, the coefficient of viscosity of the solution is $10\text{Pas}$ .

questions.question_text: The area of cross section of the rope used to lift a load by a crane is $2.5 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$ . The maximum lifting capacity of the crane is 10 metric tons. To increase the lifting capacity of the crane to 25 metric tons, the required area of cross section of the rope should be : (take $g=10ms^{-2}$ )
questions.question_html:
The area of cross section of the rope used to lift a load by a crane is $2.5 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$ . The maximum lifting capacity of the crane is 10 metric tons. To increase the lifting capacity of the crane to 25 metric tons, the required area of cross section of the rope should be :

(take $g=10ms^{-2}$ )
questions.explanation_text: The relationship between stress (σ), force (F), and area (A) is given by : $\sigma=\frac{F}{A}$ In this context, the force is equal to the weight of the load, so we can substitute force with mass (m) times gravity (g) : $F=m \cdot g$ From this, we get the formula for the cross-sectional area required to support a given mass : $A=\frac{F}{\sigma}=\frac{m \cdot g}{\sigma}$ We can set up a proportionality relationship between the area for 10 metric tons (A₁₀) and the area for 25 metric tons (A₂₅) as follows : $\frac{A_{10}}{A_{25}}=\frac{m_{10}}{m_{25}}$ Using the given values : $A_{10}=2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ m², $m_{10}=10,000$ kg, $m_{25}=25,000$ kg, Solving for $A_{25}$ : $A_{25}=A_{10} \times (\frac{m_{25}}{m_{10}})=2.5 \times 10^{-4}m^{2} \times (\frac{25,000kg}{10,000kg})=6.25 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$ So, Option A $(6.25 \times 10^{-4}m^{2})$ is the correct answer.
questions.explanation_html:
The relationship between stress (σ), force (F), and area (A) is given by :

$\sigma=\frac{F}{A}$

In this context, the force is equal to the weight of the load, so we can substitute force with mass (m) times gravity (g) :

$F=m \cdot g$

From this, we get the formula for the cross-sectional area required to support a given mass :

$A=\frac{F}{\sigma}=\frac{m \cdot g}{\sigma}$

We can set up a proportionality relationship between the area for 10 metric tons (A₁₀) and the area for 25 metric tons (A₂₅) as follows :

$\frac{A_{10}}{A_{25}}=\frac{m_{10}}{m_{25}}$

Using the given values :

  • $A_{10}=2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ m²,
  • $m_{10}=10,000$ kg,
  • $m_{25}=25,000$ kg,

Solving for $A_{25}$ :

$A_{25}=A_{10} \times (\frac{m_{25}}{m_{10}})=2.5 \times 10^{-4}m^{2} \times (\frac{25,000kg}{10,000kg})=6.25 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}$

So, Option A $(6.25 \times 10^{-4}m^{2})$ is the correct answer.

The body acquires a speed of $5m/s$ at the bottom of the circular path. Strain produced in the string when the body is at the bottom of the circle is _________ $\times 10^{-5}$ .

(use Young's modulus $10^{11}N/m^{2}$ and $g=10m/s^{2}$ )
questions.explanation_html:
$A=4 \times 10^{-6}$ m2

$l=0.5$ m

$m=2$ kg

$v_{b}=5$ m/s

$T_{b}=mg+m(\frac{V_{b}^{2}}{l})$

$=20+2 \times \frac{25}{\frac{1}{2}}=120$ N

$\frac{\Delta l}{l}=\frac{T_{b}}{A} \times \frac{1}{Y}=\frac{120}{4 \times 10^{-6}} \times 10^{-11}=30 \times 10^{-5}$

questions.question_text: If p is the density and $\eta$ is coefficient of viscosity of fluid which flows with a speed v in the pipe of diameter d, the correct formula for Reynolds number R e is :
questions.question_html: If p is the density and $\eta$ is coefficient of viscosity of fluid which flows with a speed v in the pipe of diameter d, the correct formula for Reynolds number Re is :

options.label: A
options.html: $R_{e}=\frac{\eta d}{\rho v}$

options.label: B
options.html: $R_{e}=\frac{\rho v}{\eta d}$

questions.explanation_text: The Reynolds number (Re) is a dimensionless quantity used in fluid mechanics to predict the onset of turbulence. It is defined as: $Re=\frac{\rho vd}{\eta}$ where: $\rho$ is the fluid density $v$ is the fluid velocity $d$ is a characteristic linear dimension (for a pipe, this is typically the diameter) $\eta$ is the dynamic viscosity of the fluid So, Option C is the correct answer: $R_{e}=\frac{\rho vd}{\eta}$
questions.explanation_html:
The Reynolds number (Re) is a dimensionless quantity used in fluid mechanics to predict the onset of turbulence. It is defined as:

$Re=\frac{\rho vd}{\eta}$

where:

  • $\rho$ is the fluid density
  • $v$ is the fluid velocity
  • $d$ is a characteristic linear dimension (for a pipe, this is typically the diameter)
  • $\eta$ is the dynamic viscosity of the fluid

So, Option C is the correct answer:

$R_{e}=\frac{\rho vd}{\eta}$

questions.explanation_text: In series combination $\Delta$ l = l 1 + l 2 $Y=\frac{F/A}{\Delta l/l} \Rightarrow \Delta l=\frac{Fl}{AY}$ $\Rightarrow \Delta l∝\frac{l}{Y}$ Equivalent length of rod after joining is = 2l As, lengths are same and force is also same in series $\Delta l=\Delta l_{1}+\Delta l_{2}$ $\frac{l_{eq}}{Y_{eq}}=\frac{l}{Y_{1}}+\frac{l}{Y_{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{2l}{Y}=\frac{l}{Y_{1}}+\frac{l}{Y_{2}}$ $\therefore$ $Y=\frac{2Y_{1}Y_{2}}{Y_{1}+Y_{2}}$
questions.explanation_html:
In series combination $\Delta$ l = l1 + l2

$Y=\frac{F/A}{\Delta l/l} \Rightarrow \Delta l=\frac{Fl}{AY}$

$\Rightarrow \Delta l∝\frac{l}{Y}$

Equivalent length of rod after joining is = 2l

As, lengths are same and force is also same in series

$\Delta l=\Delta l_{1}+\Delta l_{2}$

$\frac{l_{eq}}{Y_{eq}}=\frac{l}{Y_{1}}+\frac{l}{Y_{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{2l}{Y}=\frac{l}{Y_{1}}+\frac{l}{Y_{2}}$

$\therefore$ $Y=\frac{2Y_{1}Y_{2}}{Y_{1}+Y_{2}}$

questions.explanation_text: R is the radius of bigger drop. r is the radius of n water drops. Water drops are combined to make bigger drop. So, Volume of n drops = volume of bigger drop $n(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3})=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $R=rn^{1/3} \Rightarrow n=(\frac{R}{r})^{3}$ Loss in surface energy, $\Delta$ U = T $\times$ (Change in surface area) $\Delta$ U = T (n4 $\pi$ r 2 $-$ 4 $\pi$ R 2 ) $\Delta U=4\pi T[(\frac{R}{r})^{3}r^{2}-R^{2}]=\frac{4\pi T(\frac{R^{3}}{r}-R^{2})}{J}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{\Delta U}{V}=\frac{4\pi T(\frac{R^{3}}{r}-R^{2})}{J \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}}=\frac{3T}{J}[\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{R}]$
questions.explanation_html:
R is the radius of bigger drop.

r is the radius of n water drops.

Water drops are combined to make bigger drop.

So,

Volume of n drops = volume of bigger drop

$n(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3})=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $R=rn^{1/3} \Rightarrow n=(\frac{R}{r})^{3}$

Loss in surface energy, $\Delta$ U = T $\times$ (Change in surface area)

$\Delta$ U = T (n4 $\pi$ r2 $-$ 4 $\pi$ R2)

$\Delta U=4\pi T[(\frac{R}{r})^{3}r^{2}-R^{2}]=\frac{4\pi T(\frac{R^{3}}{r}-R^{2})}{J}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{\Delta U}{V}=\frac{4\pi T(\frac{R^{3}}{r}-R^{2})}{J \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}}=\frac{3T}{J}[\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{R}]$

questions.explanation_text: Let initial length and diameter be l 1 and d 1 , whereas final length and diameter be l 2 and d 2 . Given, l 2 = 2l 1 , d 2 = 2d 1 , $\Delta$ l 1 = 0.04 m By using formula of Young's modulus of elasticity, $Y=\frac{F.l}{A\Delta l}$ $\therefore$ $Y_{1}=Y_{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{Fl_{1}}{A_{1} \times \Delta l_{1}}=\frac{Fl_{2}}{A_{2} \times \Delta l_{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{Fl_{1}}{\pi(d_{1}/2)^{2} \times 0.04}=\frac{F2l_{1}}{\pi(2d_{1}/2)^{2} \times \Delta l_{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{1/4 \times 0.04}=\frac{2}{\Delta l_{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \Delta l_{2}=0.02$ m = 2 cm

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: Two small drops of mercury each of radius R coalesce to form a single large drop. The ratio of total surface energy before and after the change is :
questions.question_html: Two small drops of mercury each of radius R coalesce to form a single large drop. The ratio of total surface energy before and after the change is :
questions.explanation_text: The volume of a sphere is given by $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$ . So the volume of the two small mercury drops each of radius $R$ is $2 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$ . When they coalesce to form a larger drop, the volume is conserved. So, the volume of the larger drop is also $2 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$ . Let's denote the radius of this large drop as $R^{'}$ . Therefore, $2 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{'}^{3}$ . Solving for $R^{'}$ , we get $R^{'}=2^{1/3}R$ . Now, the surface energy of a sphere is proportional to its surface area, and the surface area of a sphere is given by $4\pi R^{2}$ . So, the ratio of total surface energy before and after the change is: $\frac{2 \times 4\pi R^{2}}{4\pi(2^{1/3}R)^{2}}=\frac{2}{2^{2/3}}=2^{1/3}:1$
questions.explanation_html:
The volume of a sphere is given by $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$ .

So the volume of the two small mercury drops each of radius $R$ is $2 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$ .

When they coalesce to form a larger drop, the volume is conserved. So, the volume of the larger drop is also $2 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$ .

Let's denote the radius of this large drop as $R^{'}$ .

Therefore, $2 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{'}^{3}$ .

Solving for $R^{'}$ , we get $R^{'}=2^{1/3}R$ .

Now, the surface energy of a sphere is proportional to its surface area, and the surface area of a sphere is given by $4\pi R^{2}$ .

So, the ratio of total surface energy before and after the change is:

$\frac{2 \times 4\pi R^{2}}{4\pi(2^{1/3}R)^{2}}=\frac{2}{2^{2/3}}=2^{1/3}:1$

questions.question_html: The normal density of a material is $\rho$ and its bulk modulus of elasticity is K. The magnitude of increase in density of material, when a pressure P is applied uniformly on all sides, will be :
questions.explanation_text: Bulk modulus $K=\frac{-\Delta P}{\frac{\Delta v}{v}}=\frac{-\Delta Pv}{\Delta v}$ We know, $\rho=\frac{M}{V}$ So, $\frac{-\Delta\rho}{\rho}=\frac{\Delta v}{v}$ $K=\frac{-\Delta P}{(-\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho})}=\frac{\rho\Delta P}{\Delta\rho}$ $\Delta\rho=\frac{\rho\Delta P}{K}$ $\Delta\rho=\frac{\rho P}{K}$
questions.explanation_html:
Bulk modulus $K=\frac{-\Delta P}{\frac{\Delta v}{v}}=\frac{-\Delta Pv}{\Delta v}$

We know, $\rho=\frac{M}{V}$

So, $\frac{-\Delta\rho}{\rho}=\frac{\Delta v}{v}$

$K=\frac{-\Delta P}{(-\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho})}=\frac{\rho\Delta P}{\Delta\rho}$

$\Delta\rho=\frac{\rho\Delta P}{K}$

$\Delta\rho=\frac{\rho P}{K}$

questions.question_html:
Consider a water tank as shown in the figure. It's cross-sectional area is 0.4 m2. The tank has an opening B near the bottom whose cross-section area is 1 cm2. A load of 24 kg is applied on the water at the top when the height of the water level is 40 cm above the bottom, the velocity of water coming out the opening B is v ms-1.

The value of v, to the nearest integer, is ___________. [Take value of g to be 10 ms-2]
questions.explanation_text: Force at point A, mg + p 0 A = pA $\Rightarrow$ p = p 0 + $\frac{mg}{A}$ Given, area of A = 0.4 m 2 = 0.4 $\times$ 10 4 cm 2 and area of B = 1 cm 2 applying continuity equation AV 1 = av [V 1 = velocity at point A] $\Rightarrow$ V 1 = $\frac{a}{A}v$ As A >>> a so $\frac{a}{A}$ very small $\therefore$ V 1 <<< v So we can neglect V 1 by assuming V 1 = 0 On applying Bernoulli's theorem at points A and B, $p_{0}+\frac{mg}{A}+\frac{\rho V_{1}^{2}}{2}+\rho gℎ=p_{0}+\frac{\rho v^{2}}{2}+0$ $\Rightarrow p_{0}+\frac{mg}{A}+0+\rho gℎ=p_{0}+\frac{\rho v^{2}}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{mg}{A}+\rho gℎ=\frac{\rho v^{2}}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{24 \times 10}{0.4}+1000 \times 10 \times 0.4=\frac{1000 \times v^{2}}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ v $≃$ 3 m/s
questions.explanation_html:
Force at point A,

mg + p0A = pA

$\Rightarrow$ p = p0 + $\frac{mg}{A}$

Given, area of A = 0.4 m2 = 0.4 $\times$ 104 cm2 and area of B = 1 cm2

applying continuity equation

AV1 = av [V1 = velocity at point A]

$\Rightarrow$ V1 = $\frac{a}{A}v$

As A >>> a so $\frac{a}{A}$ very small

$\therefore$ V1 <<< v

So we can neglect V1 by assuming V1 = 0

On applying Bernoulli's theorem at points A and B,

$p_{0}+\frac{mg}{A}+\frac{\rho V_{1}^{2}}{2}+\rho gℎ=p_{0}+\frac{\rho v^{2}}{2}+0$

$\Rightarrow p_{0}+\frac{mg}{A}+0+\rho gℎ=p_{0}+\frac{\rho v^{2}}{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{mg}{A}+\rho gℎ=\frac{\rho v^{2}}{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{24 \times 10}{0.4}+1000 \times 10 \times 0.4=\frac{1000 \times v^{2}}{2}$

questions.question_html: The value of tension in a long thin metal wire has been changed from T1 to T2. The lengths of the metal wire at two different values of tension T1 and T2 are l1 and l2 respectively. The actual length of the metal wire is :
questions.explanation_text: Suppose, I 0 be the actual length of metal wire and Y be its Young's modulus. From Hooke's law, $Y=\frac{TI_{0}}{A\Delta I}$ where, $\Delta I=I-I_{0}$ $\Rightarrow Y=\frac{TI_{0}}{A(I-I_{0})}$ or $I-I=\frac{TI_{0}}{AY}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{I_{1}-I_{0}}{I_{2}-I_{0}}=\frac{T_{1}I_{0}}{AY} \times \frac{AY}{T_{2}I_{0}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$ $\Rightarrow I_{1}T_{2}-I_{0}T_{2}=I_{2}T_{1}-I_{0}T_{1}$ $\Rightarrow I_{0}=\frac{I_{1}T_{2}-I_{2}T_{1}}{T_{2}-T_{1}}=\frac{T_{1}I_{2}-T_{2}I_{1}}{(T_{1}-T_{2})}$
questions.explanation_html:
Suppose, I0 be the actual length of metal wire and Y be its Young's modulus.

From Hooke's law,

$Y=\frac{TI_{0}}{A\Delta I}$

where, $\Delta I=I-I_{0}$

$\Rightarrow Y=\frac{TI_{0}}{A(I-I_{0})}$ or $I-I=\frac{TI_{0}}{AY}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{I_{1}-I_{0}}{I_{2}-I_{0}}=\frac{T_{1}I_{0}}{AY} \times \frac{AY}{T_{2}I_{0}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$

$\Rightarrow I_{1}T_{2}-I_{0}T_{2}=I_{2}T_{1}-I_{0}T_{1}$

$\Rightarrow I_{0}=\frac{I_{1}T_{2}-I_{2}T_{1}}{T_{2}-T_{1}}=\frac{T_{1}I_{2}-T_{2}I_{1}}{(T_{1}-T_{2})}$

questions.question_html: A steel rod with y = 2.0 $\times$ 1011 Nm $-$ 2 and $\alpha$ = 10 $-$ 5 $^{\circ}$ C $-$ 1 of length 4 m and area of cross-section 10 cm2 is heated from 0 $^{\circ}$ C to 400 $^{\circ}$ C without being allowed to extend. questions.explanation_text: Given, the Young's modulus of the steel rod, Y = 2 $\times$ 10 11 Pa Thermal coefficient of the steel rod, $\alpha$ = 10 $-$ 5 $^{\circ}$ C The length of the steel rod, l = 4 m The area of the cross-section, A = 10 cm 2 The temperature difference, $\Delta$ T = 400 $^{\circ}$ C As we know that, Thermal strain = $\alpha$ $\Delta$ T Using the Hooke's law Young's modulus (Y) = $\frac{Tℎermalstress}{Tℎermalstrain}=\frac{F/A}{\alpha\Delta T}$ Thermal stress, $F=YA\alpha\Delta T$ Substitute the values in the above equation, we get $F=2 \times 10^{11} \times 10 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{-5} \times (400)$ $=8 \times 10^{5}N$ Comparing with, $F=x \times 10^{5}N$ The value of the x = 8.
questions.explanation_html:
Given, the Young's modulus of the steel rod, Y = 2 $\times$ 1011 Pa

Thermal coefficient of the steel rod, $\alpha$ = 10 $-$ 5 $^{\circ}$ C

The length of the steel rod, l = 4 m

The area of the cross-section, A = 10 cm2

The temperature difference, $\Delta$ T = 400 $^{\circ}$ C

As we know that,

Thermal strain = $\alpha$ $\Delta$ T

Using the Hooke's law

Young's modulus (Y) = $\frac{Tℎermalstress}{Tℎermalstrain}=\frac{F/A}{\alpha\Delta T}$

Thermal stress, $F=YA\alpha\Delta T$

Substitute the values in the above equation, we get

$F=2 \times 10^{11} \times 10 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{-5} \times (400)$

$=8 \times 10^{5}N$

Comparing with, $F=x \times 10^{5}N$

The value of the x = 8.

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{I_{a}}{I_{b}}=\frac{r_{a}^{2} \times \Delta I_{a}}{r_{b}^{2} \times \Delta I_{b}}=\frac{r_{a}^{2} \times 2}{(4r_{a})^{2} \times 4}=\frac{r_{a}^{2}}{16r_{a}^{2} \times 2}$

mg = Fb

questions.question_html:
Water flows in a horizontal tube (see figure).

questions.explanation_text: Rate of flow of water is same at both A and B A A V A = A B V B (40)V A = (20)V B V B = 2V A .......(1) Using Bernoulli's theorem P A + $\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{A}^{2}$ = P B + $\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{B}^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ P A - P B = $\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{B}^{2}$ - $\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{A}^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ 700 = $\frac{1}{2} \times 1000(4V_{A}^{2}-V_{A}^{2})$ $\Rightarrow$ V A = 0.68 m/s = 68 cm/s $\therefore$ Flow rate = A A V A = (40)(68) = 2720 cm 3 /s
questions.explanation_html:
Rate of flow of water is same at both A and B

AAVA = ABVB

(40)VA = (20)VB

VB = 2VA .......(1)

Using Bernoulli's theorem

PA + $\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{A}^{2}$ = PB + $\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{B}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ PA - PB = $\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{B}^{2}$ - $\frac{1}{2}\rho V_{A}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ 700 = $\frac{1}{2} \times 1000(4V_{A}^{2}-V_{A}^{2})$

$\Rightarrow$ VA = 0.68 m/s = 68 cm/s

$\therefore$ Flow rate = AAVA = (40)(68) = 2720 cm3/s

questions.explanation_text: For a simple pendulum T = $2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g_{err}}}$ Situation 1: when pendulum is in air $\rightarrow$ g eff = g Situation 2:when pendulum is in liquid $\rightarrow$ g eff = $(1-\frac{\rho_{liquid}}{\rho_{body}})=g(1-\frac{1}{16})=\frac{15g}{16}$ So, $\frac{T^{^{'}}}{T}=\frac{2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{15g/16}}}{2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}}$ $\Rightarrow T^{^{'}}=\frac{4T}{\sqrt{15}}$

$\Rightarrow T^{^{'}}=\frac{4T}{\sqrt{15}}$

questions.question_html: A uniform cylindrical rod of length L and radius r, is made from a material whose Young’s modulus of Elasticity equals Y. questions.explanation_text: Change in length due to temperature change, $\Delta$ $l$ = $l$ $\alpha$ $\Delta$ T $\frac{\Delta l}{l}$ = $\alpha$ T [ Here $\Delta$ T = T ] Y = $\frac{\frac{F}{\pi r^{2}}}{\frac{\Delta l}{l}}$ = $\frac{\frac{F}{\pi r^{2}}}{\alpha T}$ $\Rightarrow$ Y = $\frac{F}{\pi r^{2}\alpha T}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ = $\frac{F}{\pi r^{2}YT}$ We know, The coefficient of volume expansion ( $\gamma$ ) = 3 $\alpha$ $\therefore$ $\gamma$ = $\frac{3F}{\pi r^{2}YT}$
questions.explanation_html:
Change in length due to temperature change,

$\Delta$ $l$ = $l$ $\alpha$ $\Delta$ T

$\frac{\Delta l}{l}$ = $\alpha$ T [ Here $\Delta$ T = T ]

Y = $\frac{\frac{F}{\pi r^{2}}}{\frac{\Delta l}{l}}$

= $\frac{\frac{F}{\pi r^{2}}}{\alpha T}$

$\Rightarrow$ Y = $\frac{F}{\pi r^{2}\alpha T}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ = $\frac{F}{\pi r^{2}YT}$

We know, The coefficient of volume expansion ( $\gamma$ ) = 3 $\alpha$

$\therefore$ $\gamma$ = $\frac{3F}{\pi r^{2}YT}$

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text:
A submarine experiences a pressure of 5.05 × 10 6 Pa at a depth of d 1 in a sea. When it goes further to a depth
of d 2 , it experiences a pressure of 8.08 × 10 6 Pa. Then d 2 –d 1 is approximately (density of water = 10 3 kg/m 3 and acceleration due to gravity = 10 ms –2 ) :
questions.question_html: A submarine experiences a pressure of 5.05 × 106 Pa at a depth of d1 in a sea. When it goes further to a depth of d2, it experiences a pressure of 8.08 × 106 Pa. Then d2 –d1 is approximately (density of water = 103 kg/m3 and acceleration due to gravity = 10 ms–2 ) :
questions.explanation_text: The pressure experienced by a submarine at a certain depth in the sea is given by the formula: $P=\rho gℎ$ where: $P$ is the pressure $\rho$ is the density of the fluid (sea water in this case) $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity $ℎ$ is the height (or depth in this case) Given: $\rho=10^{3}kg/m^{3}$ $g=10m/s^{2}$ We are looking for the difference in depth, $d_{2}-d_{1}$ , which corresponds to the difference in pressure $\Delta P$ : $\Delta P=P_{2}-P_{1}=\rho g(d_{2}-d_{1})$ Rearranging the above equation, we get: $d_{2}-d_{1}=\frac{\Delta P}{\rho g}$ Given: $P_{2}=8.08 \times 10^{6}Pa$ $P_{1}=5.05 \times 10^{6}Pa$ $\Delta P=P_{2}-P_{1}=8.08 \times 10^{6}Pa-5.05 \times 10^{6}Pa=3.03 \times 10^{6}Pa$ So, $d_{2}-d_{1}=\frac{3.03 \times 10^{6}Pa}{10^{3}kg/m^{3} \times 10m/s^{2}}=303m$ The closest answer among the options provided is Option C, 300 m.
questions.explanation_html:
The pressure experienced by a submarine at a certain depth in the sea is given by the formula:

$P=\rho gℎ$

where:

  • $P$ is the pressure
  • $\rho$ is the density of the fluid (sea water in this case)
  • $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity
  • $ℎ$ is the height (or depth in this case)

Given:

  • $\rho=10^{3}kg/m^{3}$
  • $g=10m/s^{2}$

We are looking for the difference in depth, $d_{2}-d_{1}$ , which corresponds to the difference in pressure $\Delta P$ :

$\Delta P=P_{2}-P_{1}=\rho g(d_{2}-d_{1})$

Rearranging the above equation, we get:

$d_{2}-d_{1}=\frac{\Delta P}{\rho g}$

Given:

  • $P_{2}=8.08 \times 10^{6}Pa$
  • $P_{1}=5.05 \times 10^{6}Pa$

$\Delta P=P_{2}-P_{1}=8.08 \times 10^{6}Pa-5.05 \times 10^{6}Pa=3.03 \times 10^{6}Pa$

So,

$d_{2}-d_{1}=\frac{3.03 \times 10^{6}Pa}{10^{3}kg/m^{3} \times 10m/s^{2}}=303m$

The closest answer among the options provided is Option C, 300 m.

questions.question_html: Young's moduli of two wires A and B are in the ratio 7 : 4. Wire A is 2 m long and has radius R. Wire B is 1.5 m long and has radius 2 mm. If the two wires stretch by the same length for a given load, then the value of R is close to :-
questions.explanation_text: Given: $\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{7}{4};L_{A}=2m;A_{A}=\pi R^{2}$ $\frac{F}{A}=Y(\frac{l}{L});L_{B}=1.5m;A_{B}=\pi(2mm)^{2}$ given F and $l$ are same $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{AY}{L}$ is same $\frac{A_{A}Y_{A}}{L_{A}}=\frac{A_{B}Y_{B}}{L_{B}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{(\pi R^{2})(\frac{7}{4}Y_{B})}{2}=\frac{\pi(2mm)^{2}.Y_{B}}{1.5}$ R = 1.74 mm

$\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{7}{4};L_{A}=2m;A_{A}=\pi R^{2}$

questions.question_text: A soap bubble, blown by a mechanical pump at the mouth of a tube, increases in volume, with time, at a constant rate. The graph that correctly depicts the time dependence of pressure inside the bubble is given by :
questions.question_html: A soap bubble, blown by a mechanical pump at the mouth of a tube, increases in volume, with time, at a constant rate. The graph that correctly depicts the time dependence of pressure inside the bubble is given by :

options.label: A
B
C
D

questions.explanation_text: When soap bubble is being inflated and its temperature remains constant, then it follows Boyle's law, so pV = constant (k) $\Rightarrow p=\frac{k}{V}$ Differentiating above equation with time, we get $\frac{dp}{dt}=k.\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{1}{V})$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dp}{dt}=k(\frac{-1}{V^{2}}).\frac{dV}{dt}$ It is given that, $\frac{dV}{dt}=c$ (a constant) So, $\frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{-kc}{V^{2}}$ ..... (i) Now, from $\frac{dV}{dt}=c$ , we get $dV=cdt$ or, $\int dV=\int cdt$ or, $V=ct$ ..... (ii) From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{-kc}{c^{2}t^{2}}$ or, $\frac{dp}{dt}=-(\frac{k}{c})^{t^{-2}}$ $\Rightarrow dp=-\frac{k}{c}.t^{-2}dt$ Integrating both sides, we get $\int dp=-\frac{k}{c}\int t^{-2}dt$ $p=-\frac{k}{c}.(\frac{t^{-2+1}}{-2+1})$ $=-\frac{k}{c}.\frac{-1}{t}=\frac{k}{ct}$ or, $p∝\frac{1}{t}$ Hence, p versus $\frac{1}{t}$ graph is a straight line, which is correctly represented in option (b).
questions.explanation_html:
When soap bubble is being inflated and its temperature remains constant, then it follows Boyle's law, so

pV = constant (k)

$\Rightarrow p=\frac{k}{V}$

Differentiating above equation with time, we get

$\frac{dp}{dt}=k.\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{1}{V})$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dp}{dt}=k(\frac{-1}{V^{2}}).\frac{dV}{dt}$

It is given that, $\frac{dV}{dt}=c$ (a constant)

So, $\frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{-kc}{V^{2}}$ ..... (i)

Now, from $\frac{dV}{dt}=c$ , we get

$dV=cdt$

or, $\int dV=\int cdt$ or, $V=ct$ ..... (ii)

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$\frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{-kc}{c^{2}t^{2}}$

or, $\frac{dp}{dt}=-(\frac{k}{c})^{t^{-2}}$

$\Rightarrow dp=-\frac{k}{c}.t^{-2}dt$

Integrating both sides, we get

$\int dp=-\frac{k}{c}\int t^{-2}dt$

$p=-\frac{k}{c}.(\frac{t^{-2+1}}{-2+1})$

$=-\frac{k}{c}.\frac{-1}{t}=\frac{k}{ct}$

or, $p∝\frac{1}{t}$

Hence, p versus $\frac{1}{t}$ graph is a straight line, which is correctly represented in option (b).

questions.question_text:
The number density of molecules of a gas depends on their distance r from the origin as, $n(r)=n_{0}e^{-\alpha r^{4}}$ .
Then the total number of molecules is proportional to :
questions.question_html: The number density of molecules of a gas depends on their distance r from the origin as, $n(r)=n_{0}e^{-\alpha r^{4}}$ . Then the total number of molecules is proportional to :
questions.explanation_text: Lets take an element hollow sphere of thickness dr Vol. of element dV = 4 $\pi$ r 2 dr Total number of molecules, N = $\int_{0}^{\infty}ndV$ = $\int_{0}^{\infty}n_{0}e^{-\alpha r^{4}}4\pi r^{2}dr$ Let $e^{-\alpha r^{4}}$ = t ......................(1) $\therefore$ $-4\alpha e^{-\alpha r^{4}}r^{3}dr$ = dt $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dt}{-4\alpha r}=e^{-\alpha r^{4}}r^{2}dr$ .....................(2) Taking $ln$ to the both sides of the equation (1), we get $ln(t)=-\alpha r^{4}$ $\Rightarrow$ $r=(\frac{lnt}{-\alpha})^{\frac{1}{4}}$ .......(3) Putting this value of r in equation (2), $\frac{dt}{-4\alpha(\frac{lnt}{-\alpha})^{\frac{1}{4}}}=e^{-\alpha r^{4}}r^{2}dr$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\alpha^{\frac{-3}{4}}dt}{-4(-lnt)^{\frac{1}{4}}}=e^{-\alpha r^{4}}r^{2}dr$ Putting in the integration, we get N = $n_{0}4\pi\int_{1}^{0}\frac{\alpha^{\frac{-3}{4}}dt}{-4(-lnt)^{\frac{1}{4}}}$ = $-n_{0}\alpha^{\frac{-3}{4}}\pi\int_{1}^{0}\frac{dt}{(-lnt)^{\frac{1}{4}}}$ $\therefore$ N $∝$ $n_{0}\alpha^{\frac{-3}{4}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Lets take an element hollow sphere of thickness dr

Vol. of element dV = 4 $\pi$ r2dr

Total number of molecules,

N = $\int_{0}^{\infty}ndV$

= $\int_{0}^{\infty}n_{0}e^{-\alpha r^{4}}4\pi r^{2}dr$

Let $e^{-\alpha r^{4}}$ = t ......................(1)

$\therefore$ $-4\alpha e^{-\alpha r^{4}}r^{3}dr$ = dt

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dt}{-4\alpha r}=e^{-\alpha r^{4}}r^{2}dr$ .....................(2)

Taking $ln$ to the both sides of the equation (1), we get

$ln(t)=-\alpha r^{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ $r=(\frac{lnt}{-\alpha})^{\frac{1}{4}}$ .......(3)

Putting this value of r in equation (2),

$\frac{dt}{-4\alpha(\frac{lnt}{-\alpha})^{\frac{1}{4}}}=e^{-\alpha r^{4}}r^{2}dr$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\alpha^{\frac{-3}{4}}dt}{-4(-lnt)^{\frac{1}{4}}}=e^{-\alpha r^{4}}r^{2}dr$

Putting in the integration, we get

N = $n_{0}4\pi\int_{1}^{0}\frac{\alpha^{\frac{-3}{4}}dt}{-4(-lnt)^{\frac{1}{4}}}$

= $-n_{0}\alpha^{\frac{-3}{4}}\pi\int_{1}^{0}\frac{dt}{(-lnt)^{\frac{1}{4}}}$

$\therefore$ N $∝$ $n_{0}\alpha^{\frac{-3}{4}}$

In an experiment, brass and steel wires of length 1 m each with areas of cross section 1mm 2 are used. The
wires are connected in series and one end of the combined wire is connected to a rigid support and other end
is subjected to elongation. The stress required to produce a net elongation of 0.2 mm is,
[Given, the Young's Modulus for steel and brass are, respectively, 120 × 10 9 N/m 2 and 60 × 10 9 N/m 2 ]
questions.question_html: In an experiment, brass and steel wires of length 1 m each with areas of cross section 1mm2 are used. The wires are connected in series and one end of the combined wire is connected to a rigid support and other end is subjected to elongation. The stress required to produce a net elongation of 0.2 mm is, [Given, the Young's Modulus for steel and brass are, respectively, 120 × 109 N/m2 and 60 × 109 N/m2]
questions.explanation_text: Corresponding to the stress ( $\sigma$ ) Total elongation $\Delta I_{net}=\frac{\sigma L_{1}}{Y_{1}}+\frac{\sigma L_{2}}{Y_{2}}$ $\sigma=\Delta I(\frac{Y_{1}Y_{2}}{Y_{1}+Y_{2}})$ $=0.2 \times 10^{-3} \times (\frac{120 \times 60}{180}) \times 10^{9}$ $=8 \times 10^{6}\frac{N}{m^{2}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Corresponding to the stress ( $\sigma$ )

Total elongation $\Delta I_{net}=\frac{\sigma L_{1}}{Y_{1}}+\frac{\sigma L_{2}}{Y_{2}}$

$\sigma=\Delta I(\frac{Y_{1}Y_{2}}{Y_{1}+Y_{2}})$

$=0.2 \times 10^{-3} \times (\frac{120 \times 60}{180}) \times 10^{9}$

$=8 \times 10^{6}\frac{N}{m^{2}}$

Water from a pipe is coming at a rate of
100 litres per minute. If the radius of the pipe
is 5 cm, the Reynolds number for the flow is
of the order of : (density of water = 1000 kg/m 3 ,
coefficient of viscosity of water = 1mPas)
questions.question_html: Water from a pipe is coming at a rate of 100 litres per minute. If the radius of the pipe is 5 cm, the Reynolds number for the flow is of the order of : (density of water = 1000 kg/m3, coefficient of viscosity of water = 1mPas)
questions.explanation_text: Flow rate of water (Q) = 100 lit/min = $\frac{100 \times 10^{-3}}{60}=\frac{5}{3} \times 10^{-3}m^{3}$ $\therefore$ Velocity of flow (v) = $\frac{Q}{A}=\frac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{3 \times \pi \times (5 \times 10^{-2})^{2}}$ $=\frac{10}{15\pi}=\frac{2}{3\pi}m/s$ = 0.2 m/s $\therefore$ Reynold number (R e ) = $\frac{Dv\rho}{\eta}$ $=\frac{(10 \times 10^{-2}) \times \frac{2}{3\pi} \times 1000}{1}=2 \times 10^{4}$ $\therefore$ Order of R e = 10 4
questions.explanation_html:
Flow rate of water (Q) = 100 lit/min

= $\frac{100 \times 10^{-3}}{60}=\frac{5}{3} \times 10^{-3}m^{3}$

$\therefore$ Velocity of flow (v)

= $\frac{Q}{A}=\frac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{3 \times \pi \times (5 \times 10^{-2})^{2}}$

$=\frac{10}{15\pi}=\frac{2}{3\pi}m/s$

= 0.2 m/s

$\therefore$ Reynold number (Re) = $\frac{Dv\rho}{\eta}$

$=\frac{(10 \times 10^{-2}) \times \frac{2}{3\pi} \times 1000}{1}=2 \times 10^{4}$

$\therefore$ Order of Re = 104

Let P 2 be the pressure inside the inner bubble and P 0 , the pressure outside the outer bubble. Radius of another bubble with pressure difference P 2 $-$ P 0 between its inside and outside would be :
questions.question_html: A small soap bubble of radius 4 cm is trapped inside another bubble of radius 6 cm without any contact. Let P2 be the pressure inside the inner bubble and P0, the pressure outside the outer bubble. Radius of another bubble with pressure difference P2 $-$ P0 between its inside and outside would be :
questions.explanation_text: Pressure difference inside the inner bubble, p 2 $-$ p 1 = $\frac{4T}{r_{2}}$ b . . . . . (1) And for outer bubble p 1 $-$ p 0 = $\frac{4T}{r_{1}}$ . . . . . . . (2) $\therefore$ p 2 $-$ p 0 = 4T $(\frac{1}{r_{2}}+\frac{1}{r_{1}})$ $\Rightarrow$ p 2 $-$ p 0 = $\frac{4T}{r}$ Here r is the radius of the bubble. $\therefore$ $\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{r_{2}}+\frac{1}{r_{1}}$ $\Rightarrow$ r = $\frac{r_{1}r_{2}}{r_{1}+r_{2}}$ = $\frac{4 \times 6}{4+60}$ = 2.4 cm
questions.explanation_html:
Pressure difference inside the inner bubble,

p2 $-$ p1 = $\frac{4T}{r_{2}}$ b . . . . . (1)



And for outer bubble

p1 $-$ p0 = $\frac{4T}{r_{1}}$ . . . . . . . (2)

$\therefore$ p2 $-$ p0 = 4T $(\frac{1}{r_{2}}+\frac{1}{r_{1}})$

$\Rightarrow$ p2 $-$ p0 = $\frac{4T}{r}$

Here r is the radius of the bubble.

$\therefore$ $\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{r_{2}}+\frac{1}{r_{1}}$

$\Rightarrow$ r = $\frac{r_{1}r_{2}}{r_{1}+r_{2}}$

= $\frac{4 \times 6}{4+60}$

= 2.4 cm

questions.question_text:
A solid sphere of radius r made of a soft material of bulk modulus K is surrounded by a liquid in a
cylindrical container. A massless piston of area a floats on the surface of the liquid, covering entire cross
section of cylindrical container. When a mass m is placed on the surface of the piston to compress the
liquid, the fractional decrement in the radius of the sphere, $(\frac{dr}{r})$ is:
questions.question_html: A solid sphere of radius r made of a soft material of bulk modulus K is surrounded by a liquid in a cylindrical container. A massless piston of area a floats on the surface of the liquid, covering entire cross section of cylindrical container. When a mass m is placed on the surface of the piston to compress the liquid, the fractional decrement in the radius of the sphere, $(\frac{dr}{r})$ is:
questions.explanation_text: Because of m mass the extra pressure created is, $\Delta$ P = $\frac{mg}{a}$ And Bulk modulus, $\beta$ = $\frac{\Delta P}{\frac{\Delta V}{V}}$ Given $\beta$ = K $\therefore$ K = $\frac{\frac{mg}{a}}{\frac{\Delta V}{V}}$ We know volume of sphere, V = $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{dV}{V}$ = 3 $\frac{dr}{r}$ $\therefore$ K = $\frac{\frac{mg}{a}}{3\frac{dr}{r}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dr}{r}$ = $\frac{mg}{3Ka}$
questions.explanation_html:
Because of m mass the extra pressure created is,

$\Delta$ P = $\frac{mg}{a}$

And Bulk modulus, $\beta$ = $\frac{\Delta P}{\frac{\Delta V}{V}}$

Given $\beta$ = K

$\therefore$ K = $\frac{\frac{mg}{a}}{\frac{\Delta V}{V}}$

We know volume of sphere,

V = $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{dV}{V}$ = 3 $\frac{dr}{r}$

$\therefore$ K = $\frac{\frac{mg}{a}}{3\frac{dr}{r}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dr}{r}$ = $\frac{mg}{3Ka}$

questions.question_text: As shown in the figure, forces of 10 5 N each are applied in opposite directions, on the upper and lower faces of a cube of side 10 cm, shifting the upper face parallel to itself by 0.5 cm. If the side of another cube of the same material is 20 cm, then under similar conditions as above, the displacement will be :
questions.question_html: As shown in the figure, forces of 105 N each are applied in opposite directions, on the upper and lower faces of a cube of side 10 cm, shifting the upper face parallel to itself by 0.5 cm. If the side of another cube of the same material is 20 cm, then under similar conditions as above, the displacement will be :
questions.explanation_text: Given : Force applied F = 10 5 N; side of cube x = 10 m = 10 $\times$ 10 $-$ 2 m; shift dx = 0.5 cm = 0.5 $\times$ = 10 $-$ 2 m On cube of side x = 10 cm; Stress = $\frac{F}{x^{2}}=\frac{10^{5}}{(10 \times 10^{-2})^{2}}=10^{7}$ N/m 2 Strain = $\frac{dx}{x}=\frac{0.5 \times 10^{-2}}{10 \times 10^{-2}}=0.5$ On cube of side x' = 20 cm; Stress' = $\frac{F}{x^{'2}}=\frac{10^{5}}{(20 \times 10^{-2})^{2}}$ Strain' = $\frac{dx^{'}}{x^{'}}=\frac{dx^{'}}{20 \times 10^{-2}}$ Now, it is given that the material is same for both cubes, therefore, $\frac{Stress}{Strain}=\frac{Stress^{'}}{Strain^{'}} \Rightarrow \frac{10^{7}}{0.05}=\frac{10^{5}}{(20 \times 10^{-2})} \times \frac{20 \times 10^{-2}}{dx^{'}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{10^{7} \times 10^{2}}{5}=\frac{10^{5}}{20 \times 10^{-2}}\frac{1}{dx^{'}}$ $\Rightarrow dx^{'}=\frac{10^{5}}{20 \times 10^{-2}} \times \frac{5}{10^{7} \times 10^{2}}=\frac{5 \times 10^{-2}}{20}=0.25 \times 10^{-2}$ m $\Rightarrow dx^{'}=0.25$ cm
questions.explanation_html:
Given : Force applied F = 105 N; side of cube x = 10 m = 10 $\times$ 10 $-$ 2 m; shift dx = 0.5 cm = 0.5 $\times$ = 10 $-$ 2 m

On cube of side x = 10 cm;

Stress = $\frac{F}{x^{2}}=\frac{10^{5}}{(10 \times 10^{-2})^{2}}=10^{7}$ N/m2

Strain = $\frac{dx}{x}=\frac{0.5 \times 10^{-2}}{10 \times 10^{-2}}=0.5$

On cube of side x' = 20 cm;

Stress' = $\frac{F}{x^{'2}}=\frac{10^{5}}{(20 \times 10^{-2})^{2}}$

Strain' = $\frac{dx^{'}}{x^{'}}=\frac{dx^{'}}{20 \times 10^{-2}}$

Now, it is given that the material is same for both cubes, therefore,

$\frac{Stress}{Strain}=\frac{Stress^{'}}{Strain^{'}} \Rightarrow \frac{10^{7}}{0.05}=\frac{10^{5}}{(20 \times 10^{-2})} \times \frac{20 \times 10^{-2}}{dx^{'}}$

questions.question_text: When an air bubble of radius r rises from the bottom to the surface of a lake its radius becomes $\frac{5r}{4}.$ Taking the atmospheric pressure to be equal to 10 m height of water column, the depth of the lake would approximately be (ignore the surface tension and the effect of temperature) :
questions.question_html: When an air bubble of radius r rises from the bottom to the surface of a lake its radius becomes $\frac{5r}{4}.$ Taking the atmospheric pressure to be equal to 10 m height of water column, the depth of the lake would approximately be (ignore the surface tension and the effect of temperature) :
questions.explanation_text: Given, bubble of radius r rises from bottom of lake. The radius of bubble at top becomes 5r/4. Therefore, pressure in bubble at bottom is $P_{1}=P_{0}+\rho gℎ+\frac{4T}{r}$ Pressure in bubble at top is $P_{2}=P_{0}+\frac{4T}{5r/4}$ Now, we know $P_{1}V_{1}=P_{2}V_{2}$ , therefore, $(P_{0}+\rho gℎ+\frac{4T}{4})\frac{4\pi}{3}r^{3}=(P_{0}+\frac{4T}{5r/4})\frac{4\pi}{3}(\frac{5r}{4})^{3}$ $P_{0}+\rhoℎg+\frac{4T}{r}=(P_{0}+\frac{4T \times 4}{5r})\frac{125}{64}$ Now given P 0 = 10 $\rho$ g, therefore, $10\rho g+\rho gℎ+\frac{4T}{r}=\frac{125}{64} \times 10\rho g+\frac{16T}{5r} \times \frac{125}{64}$ Neglecting effect of temperature, we get $10\rho g+\rho gℎ=\frac{125}{64} \times 10\rho g$ $\Rightarrow 10+ℎ=\frac{125}{64} \times 10 \Rightarrow ℎ=\frac{1250}{64}-10=9.53125m$ $\Rightarrow$ h $∼$ 9.5 m
questions.explanation_html:
Given, bubble of radius r rises from bottom of lake. The radius of bubble at top becomes 5r/4. Therefore, pressure in bubble at bottom is $P_{1}=P_{0}+\rho gℎ+\frac{4T}{r}$

Pressure in bubble at top is $P_{2}=P_{0}+\frac{4T}{5r/4}$

Now, we know $P_{1}V_{1}=P_{2}V_{2}$ , therefore,

$(P_{0}+\rho gℎ+\frac{4T}{4})\frac{4\pi}{3}r^{3}=(P_{0}+\frac{4T}{5r/4})\frac{4\pi}{3}(\frac{5r}{4})^{3}$

$P_{0}+\rhoℎg+\frac{4T}{r}=(P_{0}+\frac{4T \times 4}{5r})\frac{125}{64}$

Now given P0 = 10 $\rho$ g, therefore,

$10\rho g+\rho gℎ+\frac{4T}{r}=\frac{125}{64} \times 10\rho g+\frac{16T}{5r} \times \frac{125}{64}$

Neglecting effect of temperature, we get

$10\rho g+\rho gℎ=\frac{125}{64} \times 10\rho g$

$\Rightarrow 10+ℎ=\frac{125}{64} \times 10 \Rightarrow ℎ=\frac{1250}{64}-10=9.53125m$

$\Rightarrow$ h $∼$ 9.5 m

questions.question_html: A body takes 10 minutes to cool from 60oC to 50oC. The tempertature of surroundings is constant at 25oC. Then, the temperature of the body after next 10 minutes will be approximately :
questions.explanation_text: Time taken to cool from 60 $^{\circ}$ C to 50 $^{\circ}$ C = 10 minutes Temperature of surroundings = 25 $^{\circ}$ C Temperature of body in next 10 minutes = T Therefore, $\frac{60-50}{10min}=k_{B}[\frac{60+50}{2}-25] \Rightarrow k_{B}30=1$ ...... (1) and $\frac{60-T}{20min}=k_{B}[\frac{60+T}{2}-25]=k_{B}[\frac{60+T-50}{2}]$ ..... (2) Taking ratio of Eqs. (1) and (2), we get $\frac{20}{60-T}=\frac{30k_{B}}{k_{B}(\frac{10+T}{2})} \Rightarrow \frac{20}{60-T}=\frac{30}{5+T/2}$ $\Rightarrow 20(5+\frac{T}{2})=30(60-T) \Rightarrow 100+T10=1800-30T$ $\Rightarrow 1800-100=30T+10T$ $\Rightarrow 1700=40T \Rightarrow T=\frac{1700}{40}=42.5^{\circ}C∼43^{\circ}C$

Time taken to cool from 60 $^{\circ}$ C to 50 $^{\circ}$ C = 10 minutes

and $\frac{60-T}{20min}=k_{B}[\frac{60+T}{2}-25]=k_{B}[\frac{60+T-50}{2}]$ ..... (2)

questions.question_text: A bottle has an opening of radius a and length b. A cork of length b and radius (a + $\Delta$ a) where ( $\Delta$ a < < a) is compressed to fit into the opening completely (See figure). If the bulk modulus of cork is B and frictional coefficient between the bottle and cork is $\mu$ then the force needed to push the cork into the bottle is :
questions.question_html: A bottle has an opening of radius a and length b. A cork of length b and radius (a + $\Delta$ a) where ( $\Delta$ a < < a) is compressed to fit into the opening completely (See figure). If the bulk modulus of cork is B and frictional coefficient between the bottle and cork is $\mu$ then the force needed to push the cork into the bottle is :

options.label: A
options.html: ( $\pi$ $\mu$ B b) $\Delta$ a

options.label: B
options.html: (2 $\pi$ $\mu$ B b) $\Delta$ a

options.label: C
options.html: ( $\pi$ $\mu$ B b) a

options.label: D
options.html: (4 $\pi$ $\mu$ B b) $\Delta$ a

questions.explanation_text: Bulk modulus, B  = $\frac{\Delta P}{\frac{\Delta V}{V}}$ V i = $\pi$ (a + $\Delta$ a) 2 b V f = $\pi$ a 2 b $\therefore$ $\Delta$ V = 2 $\pi$ ab $\Delta$ a $\therefore$ $\frac{\Delta V}{V}$ = $\frac{2\pi ab\Delta a}{\pi a^{2}b}$ = $\frac{2\Delta a}{a}$ $\therefore$ $\Delta$ P = B $\times$ $\frac{\Delta V}{V}$ = B $\times$ $\frac{2\Delta a}{a}$ Normal Force (N) = $\Delta$ P $\times$ A = B $\times$ $\frac{2\Delta a}{a}$ $\times$ (2 $\pi$ a)b =   4 $\pi$ B $\Delta$ ab $\therefore$ Frictional force = $\mu$ N = (4 $\pi$ $\mu$ Bb) $\Delta$ a
questions.explanation_html:
Bulk modulus, B  =   $\frac{\Delta P}{\frac{\Delta V}{V}}$

Vi  =   $\pi$ (a + $\Delta$ a)2b

Vf  =   $\pi$ a2b

$\therefore$     $\Delta$ V = 2 $\pi$ ab $\Delta$ a

$\therefore$     $\frac{\Delta V}{V}$ = $\frac{2\pi ab\Delta a}{\pi a^{2}b}$ = $\frac{2\Delta a}{a}$

$\therefore$     $\Delta$ P = B $\times$ $\frac{\Delta V}{V}$

      = B $\times$ $\frac{2\Delta a}{a}$

Normal Force (N) = $\Delta$ P $\times$ A

       = B $\times$ $\frac{2\Delta a}{a}$ $\times$ (2 $\pi$ a)b

       =   4 $\pi$ B $\Delta$ ab

$\therefore$    Frictional force = $\mu$ N = (4 $\pi$ $\mu$ Bb) $\Delta$ a

$\Rightarrow$    x = r $(\frac{H}{H+g})^{\frac{1}{4}}$

questions.question_text: Which of the following option correctly describes the variation of the speed v and acceleration ‘a’ of a point mass falling vertically in a viscous medium that applies a force F = − kv, where ‘k’ is a constant, on the body ? (Graphs are schematic and not drawn to scale)
questions.question_html: Which of the following option correctly describes the variation of the speed v and acceleration ‘a’ of a point mass falling vertically in a viscous medium that applies a force F = − kv, where ‘k’ is a constant, on the body ? (Graphs are schematic and not drawn to scale)

options.label: A
B
C
D

questions.explanation_text: Equation of motion for the mass, ma = mg $-$ kv $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{mg-kv}{m}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\int_{0}^{v}\frac{dv}{mg-kv}=\frac{1}{m}\int_{0}^{t}dt$ $\Rightarrow$ $-\frac{1}{k}[ln(mg-kv)]_{0}^{v}=\frac{t}{m}$ $\Rightarrow$ $ln(\frac{mg-kv}{mg})=-\frac{kt}{m}$ $\Rightarrow$ $1-\frac{kv}{mg}=e^{-\frac{kt}{m}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{kv}{mg}=1-e^{-\frac{kt}{m}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $v=\frac{mg}{k}(1-e^{-\frac{kt}{m}})$ ma $=$ mg $-$ k $\times$ $\frac{mg}{k}$ (1 $-$ e $^{-\frac{kt}{m}}$ ) $=$ mg $-$ mg + mge $^{-\frac{kt}{m}}$ a $=$ g e $^{-\frac{kt}{m}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of motion for the mass,

ma = mg $-$ kv

$\Rightarrow$     $\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{mg-kv}{m}$

$\Rightarrow$     $\int_{0}^{v}\frac{dv}{mg-kv}=\frac{1}{m}\int_{0}^{t}dt$

$\Rightarrow$     $-\frac{1}{k}[ln(mg-kv)]_{0}^{v}=\frac{t}{m}$

$\Rightarrow$     $ln(\frac{mg-kv}{mg})=-\frac{kt}{m}$

$\Rightarrow$     $1-\frac{kv}{mg}=e^{-\frac{kt}{m}}$

$\Rightarrow$     $\frac{kv}{mg}=1-e^{-\frac{kt}{m}}$

$\Rightarrow$     $v=\frac{mg}{k}(1-e^{-\frac{kt}{m}})$

ma $=$ mg $-$ k $\times$ $\frac{mg}{k}$ (1 $-$ e $^{-\frac{kt}{m}}$ )

$=$  mg $-$ mg + mge $^{-\frac{kt}{m}}$

a $=$ g e $^{-\frac{kt}{m}}$

questions.question_html: According to Newton's law of cooling, the rate of cooling of a body is proportional to $(\Delta\theta)^{n},$ where $\Delta\theta$ is the difference of the temperature of the body and the surrounding, and $n$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of heat loss of a body is proportional to the difference in temperatures between the body and its surroundings. Mathematically, this law is often written as : $\frac{d\theta}{dt}∝\Delta\theta$ In this formula, $\frac{d\theta}{dt}$ is the rate of cooling (i.e., the rate of change of temperature with respect to time), and $\Delta\theta$ is the difference in temperature between the body and the environment. The law does not specify the temperature difference to an exponential power; it simply states a linear proportionality. Therefore, the correct answer is : Option D : one.
questions.explanation_html:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of heat loss of a body is proportional to the difference in temperatures between the body and its surroundings. Mathematically, this law is often written as :

$\frac{d\theta}{dt}∝\Delta\theta$

In this formula, $\frac{d\theta}{dt}$ is the rate of cooling (i.e., the rate of change of temperature with respect to time), and $\Delta\theta$ is the difference in temperature between the body and the environment.

The law does not specify the temperature difference to an exponential power; it simply states a linear proportionality. Therefore, the correct answer is :

Option D : one.
